A avaliação de risco e vulnerabilidade do PMAMC calculou os índices de risco climático associados a diferentes ameaças, como inundações, deslizamentos de terra, ondas de calor, proliferação de vetores de doenças transmissíveis, secas meteorológicas (com impacto no abastecimento de água) e elevação do nível do mar. O processo envolveu a construção de cenários específicos para cada ameaça, a identificação dos sistemas expostos e a análise de como esses sistemas podem ser afetados, considerando suas vulnerabilidades específicas.
Optou-se por uma abordagem centrada, em primeiro plano, na vulnerabilidade do sistema social (população), com foco na exposição humana aos riscos. Para aprofundar a análise, foi realizada uma sobreposição espacial das três ameaças climáticas mais relevantes (inundações, deslizamentos e ondas de calor) com a localização de áreas de interesse cultural, parques e áreas verdes, e as principais vias de mobilidade da cidade.
As Áreas Culturais e de Proteção da Paisagem (sistema territorial) foram consideradas pela sua relevância histórica, simbólica e turística. Já os parques e áreas verdes (sistema ambiental) se destacam por sua biodiversidade e por integrarem remanescentes de Mata Atlântica, um dos principais hotspots de biodiversidade do planeta. As principais vias de mobilidade urbana (também parte do sistema territorial) representam os eixos estratégicos para o transporte de pessoas e mercadorias, impactando diretamente a dinâmica econômica da cidade.
O Índice de Risco da Cidade incorporou ainda projeções da Lloyd's sobre perdas econômicas anuais associadas à ausência de preparo institucional frente a riscos futuros, incluindo os riscos climáticos. Para Salvador, estima-se um prejuízo anual total de 620 milhões de dólares americanos, dos quais cerca de 6 milhões estão diretamente relacionados a eventos climáticos extremos e catástrofes naturais. A Cidade está iniciando a revisão do PMAMC em 2025, o seja, é a primeira revisão após cinco anos de sua publicação. Além disso, a cidade prevê institucionalizar o PMAMC, bem como o processo de atualização e avaliação a cada cinco anos, por meio de um Decreto-Lei publicado no Diário Oficial do Município.

Actualización del Análisis de Riesgos Climáticos del DMQ (2020) a un Nivel III: modelación biofísica, el cual permite tener un mayor detalle de información espacial sobre posibles riesgos asociados a las amenazas climáticas (Movimientos en masa e inundaciones). 
El análisis de riesgo climático permite identificar de manera precisa y detallada las áreas vulnerables a los efectos del cambio climático dentro de la ciudad, lo que proporciona una base sólida para el desarrollo de políticas de adaptación y mitigación. El análisis se basó en una exhaustiva recopilación de datos útiles de 117 estaciones meteorológicas con registros entre 2004 y 2024 proporcionados por: EPMAPS, REMMAQ y FONAG. 
El análisis pone énfasis a la exposición a riesgos climáticos de equipamientos que brindan servicios esenciales para la población como: Centros de Salud, Instituciones Educativas, Mercados, Estaciones de metro, áreas verdes, entre otra. Considerando tanto valores presentes como proyecciones futuras, lo que permite una visión integral de las vulnerabilidades existentes y sus puntos críticos.
La actualización realizada acorde a metodologías establecidas en el Plan Nacional de Adaptación al cambio climático para inundaciones y deslizamientos se complementa con amenazas analizadas en el Análisis de Riesgos Climáticos del DMQ 2020. Adicionalmente, una vez identificados los principales riesgos climáticos y áreas criticas expuestas, se han definido un listado de medidas de adaptación.

The CVRA assessed how vulnerable Ottawa is to changing climate conditions and prioritized the highest climate-related vulnerabilities and risks to the City and the community. It will be used to inform the development of a Climate Resiliency Strategy and identify strategies to mitigate the greatest climate risks. 

Close to 150 potential climate impacts on the City and the community were assessed as part of the CVRA process including impacts on health and community well-being, infrastructure, the environment and economy. Through the process, about 40 priority risks were identified that require action within 1-3 years to protect the livability and prosperity of Ottawa. Priority risks are those impacts that have a medium or higher vulnerability and a medium-high or higher risk. The CVRA also identified 37 impacts that require a plan to be developed within 4-7 years and 33 impacts that require possible controls and monitoring. 

The project used well established climate vulnerability and risk assessment methodologies drawing from the Global Covenant of Mayors in Canada program. The methodology drew on knowledge from City staff, subject matter experts and key community stakeholders, as well as public input. Several surveys were distributed and a series of online workshops were held to help identify and confirm potential climate hazards, identify who or what may be impacted, and gather input on factors that affect vulnerability and consequences, including adaptive measures that are already in place. The final step in the process prioritized the top climate risks, taking into consideration vulnerability, probability and consequences.

column20: This document comprises a Hazard Mitigation Plan for Mecklenburg County, North Carolina and its incorporated municipalities. A well-prepared hazard mitigation plan will ensure that all possible activities are reviewed and implemented so that the problem is addressed by the most appropriate and efficient solutions. It can also ensure that activities are coordinated with each other and with other goals and activities, preventing conflicts and reducing the costs of implementing each individual activity. This plan provides a framework for all interested parties to work together toward mitigation. It establishes the vision and guiding principles for reducing hazard risk and proposes specific mitigation actions to eliminate or reduce identified vulnerabilities. This plan was prepared in coordination with FEMA Region IV and the North Carolina Division of Emergency Management (NCEM) to ensure that it meets all applicable federal and state planning requirements. A Local Mitigation Plan Review Tool, found in Appendix A, provides a summary of FEMA's current minimum standards of acceptability and notes the location within this plan where each planning requirement is met. As defined by FEMA, risk is a combination of hazard, vulnerability, and exposure. “It is the impact that a hazard would have on people, services, facilities, and structures in a community and refers to the likelihood of a hazard event resulting in an adverse condition that causes injury or damage.” This hazard risk assessment covers all of Mecklenburg County, including the unincorporated County and all incorporated jurisdictions participating in this plan. The risk assessment process identifies and profiles relevant hazards and assesses the exposure of lives, property, and infrastructure to these hazards. The process allows for a better understanding of the potential risk to natural hazards in the county and provides a framework for developing and prioritizing mitigation actions to reduce risk from future hazard events. This risk assessment followed the methodology described in the FEMA publication Understanding Your Risks—Identifying Hazards and Estimating Losses (FEMA 386-2, 2002).To identify hazards relevant to the planning area, the HMPC began with a review of the list of hazards identified in the 2018 State Hazard Mitigation Plan and the 2015 Mecklenburg County Multi-jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan as summarized in Table 4.1. The HMPC used these lists to identify a full range of hazards for potential inclusion in this plan update and to ensure consistency across these planning efforts. The HMPC evaluated this list of hazards using existing hazard data, past disaster declarations, local knowledge, and information from the 2018 State Plan and the 2015 Mecklenburg County Plan to determine the significance of these hazards to the planning area. Significance was measured in general terms and focused on key criteria such as frequency and resulting damage, which includes deaths and injuries, as well as property and economic damage. One significant resource in this effort was the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's National Center for Environmental Information (NCEI), which has been tracking various types of severe weather since 1950. Their Storm Events Database contains an archive by county of destructive storm or weather data and information which includes local, intense and damaging events. NCEI receives storm data from the National Weather Service (NWS). The NWS receives their information from a variety of sources, which include but are not limited to: county, state and federal emergency management officials, local law enforcement officials, SkyWarn spotters, NWS damage surveys, newspaper clipping services, the insurance industry and the general public, among others. The NCEI database contains 641 records of storm/weather events that occurred in Mecklenburg County in the 20-year period from 1999 through 2018.

Processes for prioritizing and managing climate hazards - The Program for Protection against Natural and Other Disasters addresses hazards linked to climate change (floods, storms, landslides, droughts, fires, extreme weather events) under the national risk assessment methodology. Hazards are assessed based on their frequency, intensity, and expected consequences for the population and infrastructure.

Management decisions follow civil-protection logic: (i) Mitigation: preventive measures (flood protection infrastructure, forest management, landslide monitoring). (ii) Transfer: use of state and municipal insurance mechanisms. (iii) Acceptance: preparedness for rare events where the costs of preventive measures exceed the benefits. (iv) Control: protection and rescue plans, evacuation procedures, stockpiles, training, and regular drills.

Integration with overall risk management- The Programme is the fundamental document for Ljubljana's civil protection, rescue, and disaster response. It links with Risk and vulnerability assessment, sectoral documents (such as spatial planning, health, and infrastructure), and defines the responsibilities of municipal services, public companies, and protection and rescue units. Climate-related hazards are fully incorporated into the disaster management cycle: prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery.

The methodology is based on the Law on Protection Against Natural and Other Disasters and national guidelines for preparing risk assessments. It covers physical hazards (floods, droughts, storms, fires, landslides), vulnerable population groups (elderly, persons with disabilities, children, the ill), and sectors such as transport, energy, health, housing, and public infrastructure. The Programme is implemented for the period 2023-2030, with mandatory interim updates and alignment with national documents.

The Risk and Vulnrability assessment (2025) and the Program for Protection against Natural and Other Disasters (2023-2030) together provide a comprehensive framework: with its long-term climate scenario methodology (IPCC AR5, EU guidelines), and the Program with practical, legally mandated protection and response measures. This dual approach enables the City of Ljubljana to address climate change both at the strategic level (development plans, investments, long-term policies) and the operational level (response to floods, heatwaves, storms, and other disasters).

Processes for prioritizing and managing climate hazards - The City of Ljubljana addresses climate hazards (e.g., heatwaves, floods, drought, storms, landslides, hail, air pollution, infectious diseases, wildfire risk) through the IPCC AR5 framework, defining risk as a function of hazard, exposure, and vulnerability. The assessment follows six steps: preparation of data inputs, vulnerability assessment, development of climate scenarios (RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5), exposure/impact assessment, risk assessment, and communication of uncertainty.
Identified risks are prioritized by likelihood, intensity, and impacts on vulnerable groups (children, elderly, health-sensitive groups, low-income households, outdoor and frontline workers) as well as on key sectors (transport, energy, buildings, water, health, cultural heritage).
Risk management decisions follow the mitigate-transfer-accept-control logic:
(i)Mitigation: nature-based and technical solutions (urban greening, shading, sustainable mobility, energy retrofits).
(ii) Transfer: use of PPPs and financing mechanisms to share risks.
(iii) Acceptance: monitoring and contingency planning for low-probability events (e.g., extreme snowfall).
(iv) Control: active measures such as river revitalisation (e.g., Mali Graben), UHI monitoring, and early-warning systems.

Integration with overall risk management
Risk and Vulnerability assessment is embedded in Ljubljana's broader governance system. It is linked to the Climate City Contract (CCC), primarily with the City's Program for Protection against Natural and Other Disasters (2023-2030). Processes are carried out through existing structures - the City Transition Team (CTT), Core City Team (CCT), Climate Change Council, public utilities, and 17 district communities - ensuring cross-sectoral coordination and participatory governance.

Monitoring and updating mechanisms
Two levels of monitoring apply:
Formal obligation: Risk and vulnerability assessment must be updated every five years in line with the Covenant of Mayors, ensuring alignment with EU frameworks.

Operational practice: Ljubljana complements this with quarterly updates at the level of municipal committees, annual reports to the City Council, and public consultations through the 17 district communities. This ensures continuous feedback, adaptive learning, and accountability.

Further information
The methodology combines ARSO projections, hydrological and meteorological data, socio-economic indicators, and participatory input. Unique features include the integration of cultural heritage as a vulnerable sector, the use of the Urban Digital Platform and GIS tools, and sensor networks for monitoring UHI and air quality. This multi-layered system ensures that SECAP is both strategically aligned with EU requirements and operationally embedded in Ljubljana's day-to-day risk management processes.

The Risk and Vulnrability assessment (2025) and the Program for Protection against Natural and Other Disasters (2023-2030) together provide a comprehensive framework: with its long-term climate scenario methodology (IPCC AR5, EU guidelines), and the Program with practical, legally mandated protection and response measures. The consequences of climate change are already clearly noticeable in Mannheim today. The increase in extreme weather events such as heat waves, dry spells and heavy rainfall events pose major challenges for the city. The 'Adaptation to climate change in Mannheim' concept serves as an important strategic decision-making basis and planning aid for climate protection and climate impact adaptation in Mannheim. The concept shows how Mannheim is affected by climate change/risks, defines adaptation goals and identifies 71 measures in the relevant fields of action, such as health, green spaces and urban structure.

Through management, the topics of climate impact adaptation and climate protection are anchored across departments and departments and integrated into the processes, procedures and processes of the city administration. In addition, the awareness of Mannheim's population for climate impacts is to be raised through citizen participation formats as well as educational and information programmes.

Within Mannheim, this varies greatly depending on the district: the city center (86%), Schwetzingerstadt (83%) and Waldhof-West (76%) districts have the highest proportion of sealed surfaces. Against the backdrop of the climate crisis and the associated negative effects on people and the environment, the city of Mannheim is intensifying its efforts to unseal areas in the city. Sealed soils result in the loss of important soil functions such as heavy rainfall prevention/water retention, heat and drought prevention, habitat function and soil fertility.
The unsealing concept from 2024 completes our picture of the situation by analyzing in detail where the challenges and potentials lie for the entire urban area and on a street-by-street basis. We have time to plan for a future where we have rising temperatures and may experience more extreme heat.
It is predicted that the number of hot days over 25°C will increase fourfold (to over 90 days a year) by the end of the 21st century.
The impacts of this include a significant increase in heat-related health issues and reduced productivity. It also impacts infrastructure, critical services, and our natural environment.
Heat impacts are intensified in cities by the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect, a phenomenon where urban areas experience higher temperatures than rural surroundings. Buildings, roads and other urban surfaces absorb and retain more heat from the sun compared to green landscapes. Cities also have higher population densities and human-generated heat emissions, such as heat from cooling buildings. Climate disruption and Auckland's increasing population will contribute to an increase in the Urban Heat Island effect in the future.
Heat risks across cities are not evenly distributed and not everyone is impacted equally. The most vulnerable in society, such as the elderly or those with existing health conditions, are often impacted the most.
How we are working to better understand heat impacts?
A geospatial heat dataset has been developed to provide detailed information of how temperatures vary across Auckland and the factors influencing these temperatures.
A sophisticated methodology was used for this assessment, combining two advanced climate modelling tools: WRF (Weather Research and Forecasting) and UHeat
• WRF was used to capture regional climate variation across Auckland, particularly wind, which can significantly affect UHI.
• UHeat is a digital tool specifically designed to predict temperatures and the urban heat intensity across cities at a high spatial resolution. It combines geospatial data, climate information
and a physics-based urban heat model, accounting for multiple factors that influence UHI such as land cover, building shape and size, heat emissions, and the urban climate.
A five-month period from November 2021 to March 2022 (Auckland's hottest summer to date) was modelled, producing highly detailed maps of air temperature predictions near ground level across Auckland.

Landslides are one of New Zealand's - and Auckland's - most significant natural hazards. Auckland Council has a range of strategies to proactively manage the risk from natural hazards and enhance the resilience of the region to these hazards, including landslides. As experienced in the 2023 storm events, landslides present a life safety risk, adversely affect property and infrastructure, and may damage or destroy cultural and environmental sites.
This summary report introduces a more detailed study that was undertaken across the full Auckland region to understand areas susceptible to landslides. This work was undertaken to improve our (and Aucklanders) understanding and mapping of landslide hazards across the region, and to inform more effective land use planning and planning decisions.
Landslide susceptibility models analyse different terrain features to show where landslides are more or less likely to occur. This gives us an understanding of 'what could go wrong where' (susceptibility) but not 'how often might this occur' (hazard).
The purpose and outcomes of this analysis and mapping is to:
* Provide information and collective understanding on the distribution of landslide-susceptible areas across the region, so that this can be taken into consideration in proactive land use, growth and infrastructure planning.
* Help facilitate the development of district planning regulations to allow proactive management of the risks associated with development.
* Aid and enhance regional emergency response planning.
In most cases, the best way to manage the risk from landslides is to avoid building in areas of higher risk. While the risk can be engineered out in some cases, doing this is costly and not always effective. This study does not provide information at a level of detail appropriate for supporting the design of engineering solutions for land instability. However, it can be used to identify areas where caution should be applied and where further assessment would be appropriate.

column20: 환경부 VESTAP 홈페이지에서 지자체별 기후위기 취약성 평가결과는 RCP/SSP 시나리오별로 제공 중이며, SSP 시나리오 기반의 평가항목 결과값은 계속 개발 중임 - 기후노출, 민감도, 적응능력의 가중치, 기후노출과 민감도에서 사용되는 평가지표 개선도 계속 진행되면서 평가항목 개선 시기별 차이 발생 - RCP 시나리오 기반 취약성 평가 : 기상청에서 제공하는 MME5s 앙상블 모델과 HadGEM3-RA 모델 기반의 평가 결과 값 제공 - SSP 시나리오 기반 취약성 평가 : 5ENSMN 앙상블 모델 기반으로 평가 결과 값 제공 SSP 시나리오 기반 취약성 평가항목 중 수원시와 관련성이 높고, 대표 원인 폭염, 한파, 홍수별 '폭염에 의한 온열질환 취약성(65세 이상 인구 대상)', '한파에 의한 건강 취약성', '홍수에 의한 건축물 취약성' 항목을 각각 검토(접속일 2024.7.1.기준) 폭염에 의한 온열질환 취약성(65세 이상 인구 대상)는 SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5, RCP 4.5, RCP 8.5 시나리오 기반 취약성 종합지수 상위 25% 이내에 영화동과 지동이 공통적으로 모두 포함되었고, 행궁동은 3회 중복됨 - SSP2-4.5, RCP 4.5, RCP 8.5 시나리오에서 지동은 1순위로 취약한 것으로 평가됨 - RCP 4.5에서 2순위 영화동, 3순위 매탄2동은 SSP 2-4.5 시나리오 기반 평가에서는 영화동 8순위, 매탄2동 13순위로 차이가 있음 한파에 의한 건강 취약성 평가는 SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5, RCP 4.5, RCP 8.5 시나리오 기반 취약성 종합지수 상위 25% 이내에 고등동, 곡선동, 망포1동, 망포2동, 연무동, 평동이 3회 이상 포함됨 - SSP 2-4.5, RCP 8.5 시나리오에서 연무동이 각각 1순위로 가장 취약하게 나타남 홍수에 의한 건축물 취약성 평가는 SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5, RCP 4.5, RCP 8.5 시나리오 기반 취약성 종합지수 상위 25% 이내에 평동, 매탄2동이 이 3회 이상 포함됨 - SSP 2-4.5, SSP 5-8.5에서는 평동이 2순위 이나, RCP 8.5 에서는 9순위로 차이가 있음 물부문(경기도 기준 대비 수원시의 취약성이 높은 항목은 치수의 취약성, 단기가뭄에 의한 용수 취약성(일반, 공업용수), 장기가뭄에 의한 용수 취약성(일반, 공업용수), 가뭄에 의한 수질 취약성이었음 수원시는 단기/장기 가뭄에 의한 취약성이 높으며, 특히 공업용수에 대한 취약성 및 가뭄으로 인한 수질의 영향을 낮출 수 있는 대책 마련이 필요함) 1.1.1.1.1. 산림/생태계 부문 경기도 대비 수원시의 취약성이 높은 항목은 병해충에 의한 소나무의 취약성, 산림생산성의 취약성, 산사태에 의한 임도의 취약성, 소나무와 송이버섯의 취약성, 침엽수의 취약성이었음 특히 소나무, 침엽수 관련 취약성이 높아 병해충과 식생환경에 대한 대책 마련이 필요함 수원시는 산사태에 의한 임도 취약성은 경기도보다 높고, 집중호우에 의한 산사태 취약성은 경기도보다는 낮지만 다른 항목보다 높은 값으로 산사태 대비책을 마련해야 함 1.1.1.1.2. 국토 부문 경기도 기준 대비 수원시의 취약성이 높은 항목은 홍수에 대한 건축물 취약성, 폭염에 의한 주거지역 취약성으로 나타남 수원시는 홍수와 폭염에 대해 단·장기적으로 대책의 시기별 전략이 필요하며, 취약한 시설 및 지역의 우선순위 대상으로 시설 개선, 제방 설치, 지역 관리 매뉴얼 방안이 필요함 1.1.1.1.3. 농축산 부문 경기도 기준 대비 수원시의 취약성이 높은 항목은 사과 생산성의 취약성, 병해충·질병에 의한 농작물·가축 위험관리 취약성으로 나옴 1.1.1.1.4. 산업/에너지 부문 산업/에너지 부문에서는 폭염 및 한파에 의한 냉난방 관리(비용) 취약성이 현재부터 미래까지 계속해서 취약하게 나타남 기후변화에 의한 실외 관광지(자연 및 생태환경) 취약성은 현재 보다 2030년 이후 미래 시점에서 경기도 취약성 수준보다 더 높아져, 적응대책 수립 시 검토될 필요가 있는 것으로 확인됨 1.1.1.1.5. 건강 부문 경기도 기준 대비 수원시의 취약성이 높은 항목은 미세먼지에 의한 건강 취약성, 오존 농도 상승에 의한 건강 취약성, 폭염에 의한 건강 취약성, 홍수에 의한 건강 취약성, 폭염에 의한 온열 질환 취약성(일반, 심혈관계질환자, 65세 이상 노인 대상, 5세 미만 영유아 대상, 야외 노동자 대상, 저소득층 대상), 대기오염에 의한 호흡기계‧알레르기 질환 취약성, 폭염에 의한 정신질환 취약성이 높게 나타남 수원시의 건강 부문 취약성은 전체적으로 높게 나왔으며, 시기별로 보았을 때 상승/유지세를 보여 단·장기적으로 대책의 시기별 전략이 필요함 수원시는 특히 폭염에 의한 건강과 열에 취약한 계층의 온열질환 취약성이 모두 높아 취약계층을 중심으로 열 환경을 개선할 필요 있음 또한 대기의 미세먼지와 오존농도, 오염물질로 인한 건강 취약성이 높은 편으로 대기환경 정화 대책이 필요해 보임. 기후위험 및 취약성 평가에 대한 주요 결과는 첨부한 제3차 수원시 기후위기 적응대책 보고서 내 4장 3절을 참고 바람.

-Agriculture, Livestock, and Fisheries Sector
Agriculture: Climate change leads to changes in the production and cultivation areas of major crops → increased risk of yield reduction and economic loss. Vulnerable to securing stable water supply due to heavy rains, heat waves, and droughts.
Livestock: Heat waves cause livestock deaths, reduced milk production, and worsening heat stress. Efforts include building a livestock damage database and calculating a heat stress index.
Fisheries: Decline in coastal fishery production and changes in species distribution. High water temperatures, hypoxia, and ocean acidification further threaten fishery resources.
-Water Resources Sector
Securing stable water supply is difficult due to extreme weather events (heavy rain, drought).
Agricultural water is particularly vulnerable, and the risk of water pollution is increasing.
-Marine and Coastal Sector
Increased risk of coastal disasters such as typhoons and storm surges → coastal disaster vulnerability assessment (exposure and sensitivity) conducted.
Incorporation of the latest coastal environment information, with vulnerability indices (grades 1-5) derived to establish response measures.
- Health Sector
Extreme weather events such as heat waves and cold spells increase damages to health-vulnerable groups (the elderly, children, low-income households).
Strengthening climate-health integrated monitoring systems is necessary (detailed assessments are included in the health section of the document).
- Industry and Energy Sector
Increased climate vulnerability of infrastructure such as power facilities.
Need for weather and climate risk assessments for industry-specific supply chains.

column20: Jeonju City conducted a practical climate change risk assessment in the process of establishing the 3rd climate crisis adaptation plan in 2024. The assessment consists of four stages: a literature review (Higher-level adaptation plans, research DB, VESTAP, Media searching, etc.), preliminary risk listing, final risk selection (adaptation capacity assessment), and prioritisation risks. The risk assessment was conducted through working group meetings for each of the five sectors (health, land (disaster), agriculture, water management, and ecosystem). Each working group was composed of experts, civil servants, and civil society.

According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), risks of climate-related impacts result from the interaction of climate related hazards, vulnerability, and exposure of human and natural systems. Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment for Ahmedabad includes the analysis of risks and vulnerability of urban systems and population of Ahmedabad city due to climate hazards and air pollution. This baseline assessment supported city to adopt climate sensitive urban planning, effectively manage climate change induced risks, and efficiently implement climate resilient policies and interventions. 

The Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment (CRVA) follows ICLEI South Asia's 'Towards Net Zero ClimateResilientCITIES' methodology. Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment for Ahmedabad is divided into three parts that address; i) analysis of climate trends and projection scenario, ii) assessment and prioritization of hazards and risks based on likelihood and consequences, and iii) vulnerability assessment. Inputs from the climate core team and the stakeholder committee of AMC, captured through Shared Learning Dialogues (SLDs), are considered in the assessment.

Step 1: Climate Trends and Projections
Historic climate and weather data from 1970 to 2020 was analysed to understand trends and patterns of change in temperature and rainfall. Climate projections for Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) till 2070, were derived from the State Action Plan on Climate Change (SAPCC), Gujarat 2021. This information was substantiated with inputs from experts during stakeholder consultations. Based on the trend analysis and future projections, climate scenario statements were developed.

Step 2: Risk Assessment:
Based on climate trends and projections, climate risks were identified and analysed according to the likelihood of occurrence and consequence. Inferences drawn from GIS based spatial analysis and analysis of relevant climate and qualitative information received during stakeholder consultations, informed the climate risk assessment. Information from the State Disaster Management Plan (Gujarat 2016-17) and District Disaster Management Plan (Ahmedabad 2021)corroborated the results. It was observed that the city of Ahmedabad is vulnerable to extreme heat, urban floods, and air pollution. Vulnerable urban systems due to extreme heat, urban flood and air pollution were assessed. 

Step 3: Vulnerability Assessment:
Results from the risk assessment, along with data received from various departments of AMC, and qualitative information received during stakeholder consultations and one to one meetings, were used to assess the vulnerability of urban systems and their impact on people. The impacts on vulnerable groups such as low-income populations (focusing on hawkers, street side vendors, and slum dwellers), women, children, people with disabilities and the uneducated were also assessed. Vulnerable areas were identified following spatial analysis - Maps reflecting this analysis are included. The impacts of climate risks and air pollution on basic urban services (water, wastewater, stormwater, solid waste management, transport, urban greens) and emergency services (hospitals and fire services) were examined. Ward wise complaints, by urban sector and complaint types, from AMC's Comprehensive Complaints Redressal System (CCRS), were spatially analysed; this information supported the identification of areas that are vulnerable to fragile urban systems. For each urban system, the populations that are most vulnerable are also identified and their adaptive capacity is assessed in terms of their access to resources, access to information and their capacity to respond to stresses. Hotspot areas or highly vulnerable wards were identified through a map overlay technique, wherein geospatial information on complaints, climate risks/hazards and gaps in urban infrastructure and/or services were superimposed and analysed. Details and inferences of the climate vulnerability assessment are included in section 4.3 of attached Ahmedabad Climate Resilient City Action Plan.

Please refer Chapter 4 from page number 97 to 151 from attached Ahmedabad Climate Resilient City Action Plan (Towards A Net Zero Future).

column20: The climate risk and vulnerability assessment (CRVA) for Porto was updated in 2024. The process started in 2023 and was designed to build upon the previous CRVA from the Climate Adaptation Strategy (2016). For its updating not only were considered the data related to climatic events from then up until now, but also integrated the Municipal Emergency and Civil Protection Plan, the bioclimatic study of the city (from 2022), the MMP diagnostic studies outcomes (from 2018). At the same time all municipal departments were enrolled in the process of consolidating the risks, vulnerabilities, and impacts on the several cities systems (to ensure a broader picture of the city's reality). For the design and modelling of the Porto climate projections, two climate scenarios were considered, RCP 4.5 and 8.5, to ensure possible deviations from the models and to minimize uncertainty. During this process, a wide range of essential factors were considered, which allowed for a targeted assessment of impacts and vulnerabilities focused on the most vulnerable groups and the most exposed sectors. The vulnerable groups considered include children and young people, the elderly, vulnerable health groups, low-income households, and outdoor workers, given the greater fragility of these groups in the ability to respond and adapt in situations of extreme events, while they may also present a greater exposure to risk. The impacts on the most significant sectors of the city of Porto were considered and grouped into the following: ecosystems and biodiversity (nature), water resources (where water safety issues are inserted), economy, buildings, land use planning, infrastructures and equipment and human health and safety of people and property. A climate risk assessment was conducted resulting in a summary matrix that guided the establishment of adaptation goals (up until 2050) and consequently the future climate adaptation actions. The CRVA update is integrated on the Municipal Climate Action Plan (PMAC) adaptation chapter.

column20: This report was published to draw insight from what is now commonly referred to as hazard adaptation within the context of sustainability principles for input into the development of Nashville's 2040 General Plan, NashvilleNext. It outlines a holistic approach to hazard adaptation, including using sustainability tools to better prepare for future risks. Inherent to sustainability is the concept of adding value and resiliency to a community: This requires a continuous improvement process focused on quality-of-life in Davidson County that integrates: (1) equity (the shared needs and interests of people); (2) economy (value in jobs, profit-making, and broader prosperity) and; (3) the environment (inherent resilience for life provided by Earth and its corresponding natural systems). The report emphasizes using risk management as a primary tool of adaptation due to a variety of threats that may compromise Nashville's future quality-of-life. In short, this report outlines a compelling case for the city and its people to hasten prudent steps to adapt to growing hazards through a comprehensive approach using the concepts and practices of sustainability and adaptation to successfully meet future challenges. It also compares Nashville's current initiatives to state-of-the-art standards in order to benchmark progress achieved and actions that still need to be taken.

column20: To continue its climate action efforts and become more resilient, the City of Rochester has conducted a Climate Vulnerability Assessment (CVA). The purpose of this CVA is to evaluate the City's ability to adapt to anticipated climate change impacts in order to enhance its resilience planning efforts. By understanding the impacts to Rochester's resources, operations, and community, as well as who is most affected, the City can prioritize strategies that address its climate vulnerabilities. Based on its investigation of climate change impacts, the City identified critical systems and assets, assessed their sensitivity and adaptive capacity, and ranked their vulnerability. Sensitivity level indicates the degree to which a system might be affected by the climate impacts to which it is exposed. Adaptive capacity reflects a system's ability to respond successfully to climate variability or extreme events. These two indicators combine for an overall vulnerability ranking that reflects how susceptible the systems or sub-systems are to the effects of climate change. For example, if a system's sensitivity is low and adaptive capacity is high, vulnerability is likely to be low. The planning subject areas of Infrastructure, Socio Economic, and Natural Resources served as the overarching framework to evaluate vulnerabilities and opportunities for Rochester's built environment, operational components, and services. The full CVA is published at www.cityofrochester.gov/departments/des/climate-vulnerability-assessment and highlights strengths and vulnerabilities for each system within the three subject areas. An implementation matrix is included detailing short and long term priorities and key stakeholders needed for implementations.

Urban areas serve as primary drivers of social, economic, and technological advancement, functioning as dynamic centers that are crucial for societal development. Considering that nearly half of the world's population resides in cities, these urban centers require substantial resources to meet demands for infrastructure and essential services. However, this results in significant environmental consequences.

In response to these challenges, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) launched the Green Cities Programme, which envisions a more sustainable and advanced future for urban areas and their residents. Gaziantep Metropolitan Municipality (GMM) joined the Green Cities Programme in 2021. Gaziantep's participation further strengthened its already successful collaboration with the EBRD.

Through this programme, GMM received support to develop a comprehensive action plan — the Green City Action Plan (GCAP) — aimed at achieving a sustainable and resilient urban future.

GCAP focuses on key sectors that shape Gaziantep's urban structure, including Energy, Water, Solid Waste, Transport, Land Use, Buildings, Industry, and Climate Action. The plan also considers how cross-cutting themes such as climate change, gender inclusion, and smart development impact these sectors. With this detailed action plan and EBRD's support, Gaziantep reflects a visionary commitment to sustainable urbanization, aiming to transform its urban fabric and improve the quality of life for its citizens.

Aligned with the Green City Vision and Strategic Objectives — and addressing sector-specific challenges — a comprehensive list of over 100 potential actions was developed. These actions were carefully assessed using a variety of criteria, including their potential to improve socio-economic outcomes and to advance inclusive themes such as gender equality and social inclusion.

From this long list, 31 priority actions were selected to be further developed in detail. Nearly all of these actions incorporate or directly target cross-cutting themes such as climate action, digital/smart maturity, gender equality, and social inclusion.

The GCAP is structured under the following key focus areas, with actions grouped accordingly:

Water

Energy

Solid Waste

Transport

Land Use

Buildings

Industry

Climate Action

As part of the GCAP's short-list of 31 project cards, the responsible stakeholders for each action were identified through workshops held during the project phase. Following these workshops, each relevant institution officially designated a responsible person referred to as a “Green Champion.”

To monitor progress of GCAP actions, an annual update of the GCAP Monitoring and Progress Table must be submitted to the EBRD. The responsibility for updating this table lies with the Green Champions. Every year, they are expected to track and report the progress of the actions they are responsible for, in coordination with their respective municipal departments.

column20: The assessment of vulnerability of Krakow, its sectors and their components was carried out on the basis of the analysis of the effects of climate change in the city (climate phenomena and their derivatives), sensitivity assessment and assessment of the adaptation potential. Climate change characteristics were developed on the basis of meteorological and hydrological data from 1981-2015 obtained from IMGW-PIB (Institute of Meteorology and Water Management). The risk analysis was performed on the basis of determining the probability of the occurrence of climatic phenomena posing the greatest threat to the city and the expected effects of these phenomena. The level of risk was assessed on a four-point scale (very high, high, medium, low). The assessment took into account the sectors selected as the most vulnerable to climate change. The results of the risk analysis indicate those components in sensitive sectors for which the planned adaptation actions will have the highest priority. For the year 2023, a report was prepared on the implementation of the actions included in the Adaptation Plan of the City of Krakow to Climate Change until 2030

The Municipal Urban Development Program of Hermosillo is the urban planning tool covering the entire municipality, incorporating analyses for all rural and urban human settlements. Through participatory diagnosis, residents identified problems and needs related to climate change, service infrastructure, health impacts, and productive processes.

The program's general objective is to create an organized municipality with a prosperous, functional human settlement system. Hermosillo is positioned as a regional center, complemented by the population centers of Miguel Alemán and Bahía de Kino, and a network of rural localities connected by roads and highways. This framework aims to provide inclusive, accessible, and affordable mobility, maximize territorial potential, and foster optimal conditions for human activities in an environment of equity, respect for human rights, and adherence to the rule of law. The goal is to build economically viable, socially just, and environmentally sustainable communities that respect biodiversity and ecosystems, prevent and reduce risks, and enhance resilience.

The program integrates urban zoning as a regulatory foundation for developing strategies and actions, including four transversal strategies:
• Comprehensive disaster risk and resilience management
• Mitigation and adaptation to climate change
• Active environmental conservation
• Gender equality and social inclusion

Additionally, it includes 19 thematic strategies:
• Efficient territorial planning and organization
• Densification and mixed-use development
• Comprehensive risk management and adaptation
• Equitable, universal, sustainable, and efficient urban mobility
• Connectivity between rural and urban localities
• Digital connectivity
• Climate change adaptation
• Efficient water management
• Environmental resilience and green infrastructure
• Efficient waste management and circular economy
• Access to health, education, and sports
• Full coverage of basic public services
• Green public spaces and complete streets
• Economic competitiveness and tourism
• Requalification of the territory
• Promotion of local cultures and artistic expressions in public spaces
• Facilities for vulnerable groups
• Regeneration of urban macroneighborhoods
• Sustainable development of rural localities and indigenous peoples

The program outlines intervention actions, including promoting renewable energy use and production, establishing energy efficiency regulations, densifying urban areas, creating urban and rural environmental conservation zones, and improving service infrastructure and mobility. It emphasizes attention to vulnerable groups and prioritizes actions to reduce risks associated with hydrometeorological phenomena.

Additionally, it establishes instruments for financing infrastructure, forestry, and urban equipment.

• Updating and publishing the Municipal Climate Action Program.
• Developing a voluntary clean energy program with industries.
• Designing and implementing an energy efficiency and renewable energy program for municipal facilities.
• Strengthening comprehensive and sustainable solid waste management.

These initiatives are being addressed through the development of a Circular Economy Center project and the 'Metropolitan Eco-Park' forestation and economic activation project, aimed at restoring heritage neighborhoods in the historic downtown and creating a carbon sink.

La vulnerabilidad social expresa la capacidad diferencial de las personas o grupos para anticipar, resistir y recuperarse de impactos adversos, determinada por factores estructurales como ingresos, vivienda, acceso a salud y educación, empleo, género, edad o discapacidad.
La Secretaría de Políticas Sociales y Desarrollo Humano, a través de su Observatorio Social, elaboró el Índice de Vulnerabilidad Social (IVS) de la Ciudad de Córdoba, herramienta estadística que identifica áreas y poblaciones con mayores carencias relativas mediante variables sociodemográficas del Censo Nacional 2022.
El IVS integra cuatro dimensiones:
NBI/Vivienda: hacinamiento crítico, viviendas precarias, falta de conexión a servicios y de acceso a internet.
Educación: jóvenes sin secundario completo, inasistencia escolar y bajo clima educativo.
Salud: personas sin cobertura médica.
Empleo: desocupación e informalidad juvenil, jóvenes NiNiNi.
El índice se representa en un mapa que clasifica los barrios en cinco niveles de vulnerabilidad: muy alta (rojo), alta (naranja), media (amarillo), baja (verde claro) y muy baja (verde oscuro).
En articulación con el Grupo de Calor Urbano del IDI-DS (Universidad Blas Pascal), se incorporó la Caracterización de Islas de Calor Urbano (UTFVI), que identifica zonas con mayor acumulación térmica. La integración del IVS con estos datos, sumada a la densidad de personas mayores y electrodependientes, permitió desarrollar el Mapa de Vulnerabilidad Social frente al Calor, que combina dimensiones sociales, ambientales y sanitarias.
Esta herramienta identifica zonas con riesgo alto, muy alto y extremo, priorizando barrios para la acción municipal: prioridad 1 (riesgo extremo), 2 (muy alto) y 3 (alto). El mapa brinda una base técnica y territorial para orientar intervenciones, asignar recursos equitativamente y fortalecer la planificación urbana adaptativa frente al cambio climático.

column20: Los estudios técnicos que fueron incluidos en el Plan Local de Acción Climática Rosario 2030 procedentes de diferentes fuentes académicas abarcaron los siguientes temas: 1- Mapa de riesgo de inundación de Rosario, como herramienta de análisis de forma cartográfica que identifica zonas de mayor a menor riesgo y muestra la distribución espacial del posible efecto o impacto de una amenaza ante determinadas condiciones de vulnerabilidad. Contiene información cualitativa y cuantitativa sobre la probabilidad de estos eventos y medir el daño potencial asociado a su ocurrencia. Permite prevenir situaciones futuras de riesgo adecuando la gestión del territorio, y anticipando los mecanismos de actuación correspondientes a la fase de preparación ante una emergencia. 2- Índice de vulnerabilidad ante amenaza de inundaciones, análisis que tiene por objetivo cuantificar y caracterizar la vulnerabilidad frente a la amenaza de inundaciones en la ciudad, de tal forma que se puedan llevar a cabo medidas preventivas y evitar daños perjudiciales para la población y los recursos naturales. 3- Estudio de variabilidad climática, eventos extremos y escenarios climáticos futuros, presenta un diagnóstico y proyecciones climáticas futuras de corto, mediano y largo plazo (a los años 2035, 2065 y 2100). Dichas proyecciones muestran el incremento de temperaturas y precipitaciones con intensidad variable. 4- Impacto en la salud y en las inundaciones del cambio climático, pronostica un incremento de la incidencia porcentual de enfermedades y su relación con la temperatura ambiente. Tanto el primer y cuarto análisis se encuentran publicados en el PLAC (en las págs. 28 y 217, respectivamente), mientras que el segundo y tercer estudio, anexamos los informes completos. Cabe destacar que, Rosario cuenta además, con un instrumento de monitoreo que establece una línea de base de medición sobre el nivel de actual de resiliencia en la ciudad, que es la Herramienta de Autoevaluación para la resiliencia frente a desastres a nivel local. Dicha herramienta de evaluación ha permitido incrementar la capacidad de la ciudad de comprender los riesgos de desastre, mitigarlos y responder a ello; minimizando en el futuro inmediato y en el largo plazo la pérdida de vidas y las afectaciones a los medios de vida, las propiedades, la infraestructura, las actividades económicas y el ambiente. Está estructurada alrededor de los “10 Aspectos Esenciales para Desarrollar Ciudades Resilientes”. El primer monitoreo se realizó en el año 2017, y se actualizó en el año 2020. En los años 2023 y 2024 se actualizó el diagnóstico de amenazas del cambio climático mediante la elaboración de nuevos mapas de riesgos. Estos mapas se presentan de manera cartográfica, incluyendo información cualitativa y cuantitativa sobre los riesgos existentes en el territorio, que permitan orientar las medidas de gestión integral del riesgo con énfasis en las fases de prevención y mitigación. \nEn el 2023 se identificaron 13 riesgos climáticos con potenciales efectos, tales como, riesgo de afectación de la vivienda y hábitat, a la salud, asociado a precipitaciones torrenciales, a altas temperaturas, por inundaciones, etc. A su vez, se realizaron talleres participativos que permitieron identificar las principales vulnerabilidades y exposiciones de cada territorio. Estos nuevos mapas se realizaron con el apoyo del NAP Global Network y la Dirección Nacional de Cambio Climático.

column20: El riesgo sólo existe en combinación de tres elementos en el territorio: el peligro, la presencia de agentes afectables y la vulnerabilidad (CENAPRED, 2022). El estudio de la convergencia de estos tres elementos en el territorio resulta indispensable para prevenir los desastres y sus repercusiones sobre la población y sus bienes, y la infraestructura. En este sentido, los Atlas de Riesgos son instrumentos que sirven como base de conocimiento del territorio y de los peligros que pueden afectar a la población y a la infraestructura en el sitio, pero también, son herramientas que permiten realizar una mejor planeación del desarrollo urbano y económico, para contar con infraestructura más segura y contribuir a la toma de decisiones en la reducción de riesgos de desastres. Adicionalmente, la actualización de los Atlas de Riesgos cobra cada vez mayor importancia a la luz de dos tendencias recientes a nivel global: el acelerado proceso de urbanización y el incremento en la recurrencia e intensidad de los efectos del cambio climático. En entornos de urbanización expansiva como en el caso de la zona metropolitana de Mérida, con un ritmo de crecimiento del área urbana a razón de 1.4 veces el incremento poblacional entre 2015 y 2020, la comprensión de los fenómenos geológicos debe ser parte central de las decisiones de planificación urbana. De la misma forma, en la medida en que los fenómenos climatológicos extremos cobran relevancia por su intensidad y frecuencia en todo el planeta, los desastres asociados a ellos serán cada vez más frecuentes y por ello, también requieren ser contemplados en la planeación del uso del territorio, para definir medidas de adaptación y minimizar la exposición al riesgo. La implementación de acciones para la adaptación al cambio climático en México, al igual que en muchos otros países con diferentes grados de desarrollo económico, es una experiencia reciente, y existen dos aspectos importantes a considerar: a) la incertidumbre que aún existe en torno a los impactos del cambio climático (su tipo, magnitud, localización y naturaleza), y b) el dinamismo de la vulnerabilidad a los impactos, que demanda la realización de evaluaciones periódicas para comprender mejor esos procesos. En este sentido, las autoridades del H. Ayuntamiento de Mérida, a través de la Dirección de Desarrollo Sustentable, iniciaron las bases para la prevención del riesgo con la publicación del Atlas de Riesgos del Municipio de Mérida 2015-2018, particularmente enfocado a la identificación y análisis de riesgos físicos e hidrometeorológicos ante condiciones de cambio climático. En continuidad a estos trabajos, se presenta la primera etapa de la actualización Atlas de Riesgos del municipio de Mérida, Yucatán, que incorpora la identificación de fenómenos no analizados en la edición anterior, particularmente en relación con el tema de inundaciones pluviales, hundimientos, y otros fenómenos de origen antropogénico, como el almacenamiento y transporte de sustancias peligrosas, o las concentraciones masivas de población. De esta forma, se refuerza la política de gestión de riesgo en el municipio de Mérida, incorporando información más actualizada, y el análisis de fenómenos de reciente aparición o intensificación derivado de las condiciones climáticas, el crecimiento y densificación de las zonas urbanas, y la construcción de nueva infraestructura. Es importante mencionar que la versión final de este análisis estará en el mes de Agosto.

tomando en consideración el análisis de las condiciones que se han observado en los últimos

O Plano de Ação Climática de Santos - PACS foi aprovado por meio do Decreto Municipal nº 9.567, de 13 de janeiro de 2022.
Consultores/as: Ivan Carlos Maglio, Pedro Ivo Camarinha, Vitor Zanetti, Cristiane Moura, Leila Soraya Menezes, Danielle Almeida Carvalho, Wolfram Lange
Assessoria Técnica: GIZ Brasil (Agência de Cooperação para o Desenvolvimento Sustentável da Alemanha), no âmbito do ProAdapta.
Comissão Municipal de Adaptação à Mudança do CLIMA - CMMC, coordenada pela Secretaria de Meio Ambiente - SEMAM da Prefeitura Municipal de Santos, composta por representantes de diversos setores da administração municipal e convidados/as representantes da Comissão Consultiva Técnica Acadêmica - CCTA.
Os/as conselheiros/as do Conselho Municipal de Defesa do Meio Ambiente - COMDEMA também foram convidados/as a participar das atividades. Dados COMDEMA disponíveis em: https://www.santos.sp.gov.br/?q=content/comdema-conselho-municipal-da-defesa-do-meio-ambiente
A construção do PACS contou com amplo engajamento e a participação de setores muito importantes para a ação climática, como a academia, a sociedade civil, a iniciativa privada e os órgãos públicos municipais, além de uma equipe de especialistas referências na área, tornando o processo extremamente rico e repleto de aprendizados. Muitos seminários e oficinas foram realizados durante os quatro últimos anos para atingir os resultados.
De acordo com o PACS (2022) a análise de vulnerabilidade socioambiental em Santos/SP para o PACS utilizou indicadores que constituíram a base do Índice de Risco Climático e Vulnerabilidade Socioambiental (IRCVS) para melhor refletir as situações atuais do município e as atualizações dos modelos climáticos para o Brasil. Com o IRCVS, a cidade ganhou um instrumento valioso para aplicação na proposição de medidas da adaptação climática que melhor se encaixem em sua realidade.
O conceito de Vulnerabilidade Climática utilizado segue a linha de pensamento de Füssel e Klein (2006). A criação do IRCVS é parametrizada no índice SEVICA (ZANETTI et al., 2016) no contexto dos Adaptation policy assessment (Estudos de Política de Adaptação), dado que o índice em si se destina a criar um instrumento de planejamento de políticas públicas para municípios costeiros e suas políticas de adaptação climática.
De maneira a facilitar o entendimento dos papéis de cada um dos indicadores na composição do índice, dividiu-se os indicadores em dois grupos denominados: “Aspectos Físicos” e “Aspectos Sociais”.
O Índice de Risco Climático e Vulnerabilidade Socioambiental (IRCVS) foi complementado com uma dimensão de impactos do clima, que resultou das análises climáticas realizadas para o PACS (item 3.1). A consideração dessa dimensão se dá basicamente de duas maneiras: compondo os indicadores de Inundação e Movimentos de Massa; e como uma análise separada em conjunto com outras dimensões para avaliar seu agravamento ante o risco climático.

column20: The ICLEI Advancing Adaptation program has resulted in the production of a \'Discussion Primer on London's Adaptation Framework\', which was released to encourage engagement and public comment in the summer of 2024. Using a Discussion Primer approach to precede the completion of the Adaptation Framework incorporates learnings from the approach used to develop the Climate Emergency Action Plan which received widespread support including unanimous support at City Council. These external environmental representatives from Reforest London, the Thames Talbot Land Trust, Carolinian Canada and LEN were in addition to staff from the Upper Thames River Conservation Authority who assist the City in floodplain, natural hazards and natural heritage management. Virtual meeting software (e.g., Mural and Mira) and the Zoom virtual meeting platform were used which enabled input to be recorded and synthesized for the report. The report was peer reviewed by ICLEI Canada Staff. The Discussion Primer on London's Climate Adaptation Framework will lead to the completion of an Adaptation Plan to assist in implementing Workplan #8 - Adapting and Making London More Resilient and in partial completion of Workplan #6 - Implementing Natural and Engineered Climate Solutions and Carbon Capture which both form part of the CEAP. column20:
No âmbito da elaboração da EMAAC de Matosinhos foi realizado um levantamento das vulnerabilidades climáticas locais, para perceber como estes eventos adversos afetaram as atividades, as pessoas e as infraestruturas do concelho. 
No Município de Matosinhos foram identificados quatro tipos de eventos climáticos adversos distintos, no período em análise: galgamento costeiro; precipitação excessiva (cheias e inundações); temperaturas baixas/ondas de frio; tempestades/tornados; e, ventos fortes.
Os impactes e consequências dos eventos climáticos identificados vão desde alterações na biodiversidade, cheias, danos em edifícios, danos para a saúde (doenças, ferimentos, morte, etc.), danos para a vegetação, danos para as cadeias de produção, danos para as infraestruturas (viárias, ferroviárias, telecomunicações, etc.), inundações, entre outros.

A precipitação excessiva (cheias e inundações) tem como principais impactos observados danos em infraestruturas, tendo como consequências aluimento de casas devolutas, aluimento de piso, buracos nas estradas, derrocada de fachadas, descoramento de terras para linha do metro, despiste de viaturas, circulação condicionada das vias, estradas inundadas, queda de estruturas metálicas, de poste de eletricidade, entre outros.
Os impactos mais notórios na sequência dos episódios de ventos fortes estão relacionados com danos em edifícios (queda de casas devolutas, queda de estruturas, etc.), danos para a vegetação (queda de árvores) e danos para as infraestruturas (queda de estruturas).
No Município de Matosinhos, os fenómenos de tempestades/tornados tiveram como principais impactos, registados no período em análise, alterações na biodiversidade (queda de árvores) e danos para as infraestruturas (risco de ruína de edifícios devolutos, queda de chapas, queda de muros, queda de telhados, queda de semáforos, etc.) 
Os impactos mais notórios na sequência dos episódios de temperaturas baixas/ondas de frio estão relacionados com danos para a saúde, nomeadamente o transporte de sem-abrigos e de animais.
Por último, relativamente aos episódios de galgamentos costeiros, tornou-se evidente que os impactos mais notórios estão relacionados com danos para as infraestruturas, com a forte ondulação marítima a provocar várias inundações.

Para o território do Município de Matosinhos o aumento previsto de temperatura será particularmente acentuado nos meses de verão 2C a 5C e no outono 2C a 4C. Os dias de verão serão muito mais frequentes assim como as noites tropicais. As ondas de calor serão mais frequentes e intensas. Já os dias de geada deverão ser menos frequentes. O verão tornar-se-á mais seco e a estação seca prolongar-se-á muito além dos limites de verão. Os resultados sugerem ainda que as secas serão mais intensas e frequentes.
É projetada uma diminuição da precipitação particularmente no outono primavera e verão. Os dias de precipitação elevada serão menos frequentes ainda que exista uma maior tendência para eventos isolados com precipitação extrema. Prevêem-se tempestades de inverno mais intensas, acompanhadas de chuva e vento forte. 
É esperado o aumento do nível médio do mar entre 0,17 m e 0,38 m para 2050 (projeção global). A longo-prazo antevê-se o aumento do nível médio do mar entre 0,26 m e 0,82 m até ao final do século XXI (projeção global). A subida do nível médio do mar terá impactes mais graves, quando conjugada com a sobrelevação do nível do mar associada a tempestades (storm surge); 

Uma vez identificados os principais impactos das alterações climáticas, incluindo as ameaças e oportunidades que eles representam, foi determinado o risco (qualitativo) para cada uma dessas ocorrências. A avaliação de risco considera a frequência de ocorrência de um evento climático e a magnitude das consequências dos impactos desse evento. O valor do risco resulta da multiplicação da frequência pela magnitude das consequências de cada impacto.
Para além de todo o trabalho de avaliação climática e de vulnerabilidades desenvolvido no âmbito do PAESC, a presente avaliação do risco climático teve ainda por base os resultados do processo de avaliação interna dos riscos climáticos desenvolvido pelo Município de Matosinhos no âmbito da elaboração da respetiva EMAAC. 
O nível de risco identificado foi baseado, por um lado, na evolução das variáveis climáticas considerando os cenários de alterações projetadas para médio e longo prazo e, por outro lado, na pesquisa e análise realizadas sobre a sensibilidade climática do território e os impactos e vulnerabilidades atuais e futuras. Partindo destes fatores, foi atribuída a classificação da magnitude das consequências dos impactos.

Os principais riscos futuros para o município de Évora estão relacionados com a disponibilidade dos recursos hídricos, quer em termos da sua quantidade como da sua qualidade. Este risco resulta da conjugação nos cenários climáticos projetados para a região de uma diminuição da precipitação média anual, concentrada num menor número de dias, com um aumento da temperatura média anual. A concretização destas projeções terá repercussões significativas nos recursos hídricos, com efeitos na sua disponibilidade e distribuição, afetando de forma transversal, direta ou indiretamente, diversos setores.
A atividade agrícola, tal como a conhecemos atualmente, sofrerá efeitos particularmente negativos, sendo de prever uma acentuada diminuição da produtividade das culturas cerealíferas e das pastagens de sequeiro que, por sua vez, se refletirá na pecuária extensiva, e consequentemente em alterações na tradicional paisagem alentejana, o montado, e na biodiversidade a ela associada.
Ao nível deste setor, os impactos económicos deverão manifestar-se em elevadas variações inter-anuais nos rendimentos, com anos marcados pela perda de parte, ou totalidade, das produções tradicionais desta região. Sendo de prever que a tendência para criar novas áreas de regadio, de modo a compensar as perdas de produtividade e o aumento das necessidades hídricas, conduzirão a um maior consumo de água para rega e a um esgotamento mais acelerado das reservas superficiais e subterrâneas do município.
A produção animal extensiva, que poderá ser favorecida pelo aumento da temperatura nos meses de inverno, contará com um período, na primavera-verão, onde a conjugação da escassez de chuva e temperaturas elevadas dificultarão o abeberamento e a alimentação do gado, por via da diminuição da produtividade e qualidade das pastagens de sequeiro, verificando-se consequentemente um aumento na necessidades de utilização de alimentos conservados.
As culturas protegidas e a produção animal intensiva serão afetadas com o aumento da frequência e intensidade das ondas de calor que influenciam diretamente o bem-estar animal e as produções em viveiros, estufas, armazenagem de produtos agrícolas, etc.
Os espaços florestais serão afetados ao nível do rendimento económico e da capacidade de proporcionar bens e serviços. Num município onde 41% da ocupação do solo corresponde a floresta dominada por povoamentos de sobro e azinho, o impacto das alterações climáticas será bastante relevante, especialmente quando associado à possibilidade do ótimo ecológico do sobreiro estar em deslocação para norte, onde esta espécie poderá encontrar um ambiente mais húmido. Considera-se que os problemas que atualmente já contribuem para o declínio dos povoamentos de sobreiro serão agravados pelo stress hídrico e pela perda de fertilidade dos solos, tornando-os ainda mais vulneráveis a pragas e doenças que contribuirão para a sua regressão e consequente perda do valor ecológico, económico, social e paisagístico a eles associado.
Os efeitos sobre os ecossistemas naturais ou seminaturais são complexos, contudo podemos considerar que as consequências sobre o montado de sobro, sobre as culturas cerealíferas e sobre os recursos hídricos afetam significativamente os principais valores naturais e a biodiversidade do município.
É de prever ainda o alargamento do período de risco de incêndio às estações do outono e primavera, assim como o aumento da frequência e da magnitude dos incêndios quer por influência dos cenários climáticos projetados quer pela previsível diminuição da atividade humana no espaço rural.
A alteração do atual clima mediterrânico, para um clima mais árido, com mais dias considerados muito quentes e mais ondas de calor, conduzirá a uma maior incidência de stress térmico, aumento do desconforto e da mortalidade sobretudo nas pessoas mais vulneráveis como crianças, idosos e pessoas fragilizadas por algumas patologias. Ainda em termos de saúde humana é de pressupor que o período de polinização das espécies vegetais que tipicamente acontecia entre março e julho, passe a ter inicio mais cedo, aumentando o período de incidência de doenças respiratórias alérgicas como a asma, sinusites e rinites associadas a concentração muito elevadas de pólenes.
Por sua vez, estas alterações podem vir a ter um impacte negativo no turismo no concelho durante os meses mais quentes, tendo em conta que os principais interesses correspondem à realização de circuitos turísticos. Esta tendência, pode ser agravada pelas previsíveis restrições ao uso de água durante esse período.
Além dos riscos económicos e patrimoniais, existe um aumento do risco de abandono de atividades que tradicionalmente moldam o território alentejano, conduzindo naturalmente a outras consequências, como o despovoamento humano, redução da gestão do espaço rural, aumento do potencial de incêndio e descaracterização da paisagem alentejana.

O Plano Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas do Município de Évora (PMAAC), desenvolvido no âmbito do projeto ADAPTA.local.CIMAC - Planeamento da Adaptação Climática Municipal do Alentejo Central, coordenado pela Comunidade Intermunicipal do Alentejo Central, foi elaborado pela Câmara Municipal de Évora com o suporte técnico-científico do CEDRU - Centro de Estudos e Desenvolvimento Regional e Urbano, Lda., com o objetivo de reduzir as vulnerabilidades territoriais do Município às Alterações Climáticas, criando as condições necessárias para a adaptação do território e da sua população.

Tratando-se da evolução natural do trabalho desenvolvido pelo Município aquando da elaboração da sua Estratégia Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas, em 2017, o PMAAC de Évora, com um carácter fortemente operacional, permitiu consolidar o conhecimento sobre o clima local, atual e futuro, sobre a incidência espacial e setorial das vulnerabilidades climáticas específicas do concelho e desenhar um Plano de Ações de Adaptação para a próxima década. 

O PMAAC de Évora constitui o mais recente instrumento ao serviço das políticas de urbanismo, intervenção social, proteção civil, manutenção de infraestruturas e desenvolvimento socioeconómico, entre outros domínios, configurando-se como um dos contributos mais relevantes do Município de Évora para as questões globais relacionadas com as Alterações Climáticas, mas sobretudo, para garantir e melhorar a resiliência e qualidade de vida deste território e das populações.

Fort Lauderdale faces unique climate challenges due to its high groundwater table, transmissive geology, proximity to the Atlantic Ocean, extensive canals and waterways, and low-lying topography. These factors increase the city's exposure to saltwater intrusion, tidal flooding, storm surge, heavy rainfall events, and sea-level rise. The vulnerability assessment (VA) identifies flooding hotspots that have current and increasing flood risk, which helps the City target investments in priority areas. Strategies to mitigate the effects of tidal flooding 'include seawall improvements, living shorelines, or controlling other tidal impacts through backflow prevention on stormwater outfalls” (p.142). The VA consultant produced hydrological modeling for various flood scenarios and produced several maps highlighting flood prone areas. 

Additionally, the assessment assists the City's efforts to prioritize addressing climate-related hazards in socially vulnerable areas by providing a table of census tracts with a Social Vulnerability Index composite score of at least 50%, indicating “a higher-than-average vulnerability, warranting prioritization in flood preparedness and response planning (p. 137).” According to the spatial analysis, these census tracts are primarily concentrated in inland areas close to I-95 (p.139). This ensures the City develops strategies that “protect infrastructure and property [and] enhance resilience of communities ... prioritizing strategies that support the most affected populations through financial assistance, social services, and inclusive policymaking ... improving quality of life and ensuring equitable access to resources and support” (p.136).

The biggest climate change impact that Tempe is experiencing is extreme heat. Tempe's Climate Action Plan serves as a guideline for the City in its planning and decision-making. The CAP focuses on reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and building resilience to extreme heat. The plans emphasize equitable cooling by investing in shade and cooling strategies that consider socioeconomic factors. Key investments include policies, programs, and infrastructure to expand shade and tree canopy, enhance urban cooling, improve access to public transit, and lower GHG emissions.

Pages 9-10 outline the qualitative data and the City's approach to building an inclusive city for a diverse population. This includes strategies at multiple scales: touch scale (which involves designing infrastructure down to the materials used); neighborhood scale (which focuses on connecting cool spaces like shaded areas and trees that help guide park and street design); and city scale (which uses census tract data to identify where to invest in this infrastructure).

The theme of extreme heat is integrated throughout the document, reflecting the understanding that mitigation and adaptation strategies are interconnected. Many of the strategies addressing extreme heat fall under the topics of Resilience Hubs and Urban Cooling and Greening. Resilience Hubs focus on both immediate and long-term heat relief by providing access to cooling centers, supporting local emergency preparedness efforts, and mapping community assets. Urban Cooling and Greening strategies include planting trees and building Green Stormwater Infrastructure, an approach to water management that aims to save money, save water, and keep Tempe cool by working with nature to reduce stormwater runoff.

The City of Tempe, Arizona State University's Healthy Urban Environments initiative, and NASA DEVELOP partnered to create Heat Priority Scores for Tempe. Rapid growth in Maricopa County—and Tempe specifically—has led to an increase in impervious surfaces, intensifying the Urban Heat Island Effect. Local climate data shows that over the past 50 years, temperatures in the Phoenix area have risen by nearly 3.6°F. In response to growing concerns about urban heat, the partnership developed Heat Priority Scores using NASA Earth observations.

Five key environmental factors were analyzed:
Land Surface Temperature
Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)
Normalized Difference Built-up Index (NDBI)
Albedo
Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI)

These were overlaid with six socioeconomic indicators at the census tract level:

Percent of population over age 65
Percent of population living alone
Percent minority (non-white) population
Percent of population living below the poverty line
Percent of population without a high school diploma
Median household income

The resulting Heat Priority Scores help Tempe identify and prioritize areas for heat mitigation and climate adaptation efforts.

The Water Resources Master Plan provides a planning framework that will ensure Tempe maintains sufficient supplies to continually meet the demands of the Water Service Area. The plan contains an overview of Tempe's water portfolio and assets, describes available supplies and demand forecasting, provides strategies and tactics to meet current and future water demands and contains an executive summary of the Water Conservation and Efficiency Program Strategic Plan and Drought Preparedness Plan. 

Water Resources Strategies:
• Prioritize utilization of renewable resources and protect Tempe's access to them. 
• Provide the highest level of water resiliency at highest possible value. 
• Acquire new sources and renewable supplies whenever feasible opportunities exist. 
• Manage groundwater rights to maintain safe-yield pumping. 
• Develop new infrastructure and maintain current assets to protect Tempe from the impacts of prolonged droughts. 
• Maintain a customized water conservation and efficiency program that utilizes targeted outreach, innovative demonstrations and measurable programs whenever possible to continually improve water conservation and efficiency in the residential, commercial and industrial sectors of Tempe's community. 
• Continue to establish water resources planning guidelines that consider the water rights status of lands slated for development and redevelopment projects.
 • Maintain a detailed and effective Drought Preparedness Plan.

In 2010, Tempe received an Assured Water Supply Designation (AWS) from the Arizona Department of Water Resources (ADWR). This designation certified that Tempe has access to sufficient water resources to meet water system demands for 100 years. Based on an evaluation of current demand forecasting and the supplies outlined in the Tempe AWS Designation, Tempe will have sufficient water resources to meet demands up to and beyond anticipated buildout in 2040. However, maintaining these supplies, and supplementing them when necessary, requires significant effort and planning. This document addresses how Tempe will meet current and future water supply challenges, while continuing to provide affordable water that satisfies the demands of the Water Service Area now and into the future.

The Drought Preparedness Plan ensures Tempe has strategies in place to predict, prepare for and react to shortages in order to meet the demands of the water service area now and into the future. 

Drought Preparedness Plan Objectives:

• Monitor drought conditions that can create shortages.
• Understand the impact of shortages on Tempe's supplies.
• Maintain the ability to adjust operations to meet demands. 

Climate studies illustrate that the Western United States has experienced cyclical periods of drought and above average rainfall for many millennia. These cycles occur at different frequencies and intensities, and result from numerous and complex factors. Despite these challenges, many communities in the Central Arizona desert have managed to adapt and thrive. Utilizing renewable resources as a primary means to meet demands is critical to sustaining life in the desert. From the first peoples that settled in the Salt River Valley who built canals, to the farmers near Hayden Ferry in the late 1890s who put up their land as collateral to tame the Salt River, to today's innovative reuse and transportation projects that provide sources of water unimaginable in the past, Tempe has a long history of responsible water use and sound water management practices. Figure 1 illustrates Tempe's typical allocation of renewable water supplies. In most years, the majority, 87 percent, of demands of the water service area are met by renewable surface water supplies provided by Salt River Project (SRP). These supplies include SRP Member supplies and New Conservation Space (NCS) water. The remaining demand is met with additional renewable supplies consisting of surface water delivered from the Colorado River by the Central Arizona Project (CAP) and safe-yield groundwater.

In addition to providing a framework to meet supply challenges, maintaining a drought management plan is a requirement for all Community Water Systems operating in Arizona that serve more than 1,850 people.

In 2002, a prolonged drought on SRP's watersheds resulted in reduced allocation (or shortage) of SRP surface water supplies. In response, Tempe developed and implemented a drought management plan, which was approved by Tempe City Council in 2004. Shortly thereafter, the drought abated and SRP allocations returned to normal. Tempe's drought management plan is routinely reviewed and updated and during the 2012 review process it was incorporated into the Water Resources Plan. 

This update to the drought management plan removes it from the Water Resources Plan and expands it to include the following information:

• Updates regarding Tempe's water supplies and demands.
• Water shortage indicators and triggers. 
• How and when a Water Shortage Response Team will be convened.
• Updated and expanded Shortage Management Stages and Measures.
• Draft language for a Water Shortage Ordinance.

The resilience assessment analyzed Fayetteville's strengths and vulnerabilities across five domains of climate
resilience. These domains must be considered as assets to create a truly resilient community: social, health, natural,
physical, and economic. These five domains, individually observed for the sake of analysis, are interconnected and
interdependent. All five must be considered and addressed to ensure for the development of a resilient city. Each
stakeholder meeting focused on individual domains, which consisted of an introduction to the topic of resilience
and sustainability, a description of three extreme climate scenarios that the City of Fayetteville may face, and the
resilience assessment. The resilience assessment portion of the meetings tasked the key stakeholders with identifying current resiliency strengths and vulnerabilities, and then prioritized each based on their significance. Next,
the stakeholders identified the most notable vulnerabilities to their specific domain. After the Climate Resilience
Assessment was complete, the stakeholders brainstormed opportunities to address challenges specific to their
domain. Once the stakeholder meetings were finished, a nine question survey was completed by the campus,
city, and community members invited to the stakeholder meetings. The purpose of the survey was to have key
stakeholders prioritize strategies that could be taken to promote community resilience.
