In 2024 the WMCA worked with the University of Birmingham to produce two climate risk and vulnerability assessment (CRVA) mapping tools, one covering the social and built environment in the WMCA area and one covering transport infrastructure in the WMCA area. The social and built environment CRVA involved bringing together climate hazard layers, layers indicating socio-economic vulnerability and an exposure layer indicating population density. Each layer is mapped and 100m grid squares and scored from 0-1 - one indicating a high risk/vulnerability and zero indicating low. The scores are then combined to show an overall CRVA score for different parts of the region. The transport-specific CRVA works similar, though this builds in and assigns criticality and vulnerability weightings to different transport networks and nodes. Both maps give a present-day illustration of where climate risk and vulnerability hotspots are most concentrated across the region's transport networks. The West Midlands CRVA is available on the West Midlands Environment & Energy Dashboard and the methodology document is also included. 

CRVA data is now being integrated into other data platforms including the West Midlands Local Area Energy Planning Plus (LAEP+) platform.

Via the UKRI-funded WM-Adapt project, the West Midlands CRVA is being enhanced to include high resolution surface water flood mapping, urban heat island mapping, health and economic impact mapping and future climate projections. This enhanced version is expected to be delivered in 2027.

The IVA assists with understanding how: - Climate change may impact valued aspects or features in the Eastern Region; and - Particular valued aspects or features may be more vulnerable than others to climate change. The IVA was developed and implemented using a collaborative approach and involved participation by the project team (comprising consultants, Resilient East working group and steering group members) and stakeholders from across the Region. Analysis of the IVA identified a series of indicators (refer Table 1 in linked report) from which areas of focus have been identified for adaptation planning. This report documents the methodology used to complete the IVA, the approach to analysing the results of the IVA and the priority areas of focus for the third and final task of Resilient East relating to the preparation of the Regional Adaptation Plan. Work to update this regional plan has commenced in February 2025.

According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), risks of climate-related impacts result from the interaction of climate related hazards, vulnerability, and exposure of human and natural systems. Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment for Bhavnagar includes the analysis of risks and vulnerability of urban systems and population of Bhavnagar city due to climate hazards. This baseline assessment supported city to adopt climate sensitive urban planning, effectively manage climate change induced risks, and efficiently implement climate resilient policies and interventions. The Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment (CRVA) follows ICLEI South Asia's 'ClimateResilientCITIES' methodology. Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment for Bhavnagar is divided into three parts that address; i) analysis of climate trends and projection scenario, ii) assessment and prioritization of hazards and risks based on likelihood and consequences, and iii) vulnerability assessment. Inputs from the stakeholders of BMC are also captured through Shared Learning Dialogues (SLDs), are considered in the assessment. 
Step 1: Climate Trends and Projections Historic climate and weather data from 1971 to 2023 was analysed to understand trends and patterns of change in temperature and rainfall. Climate projections for Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) were derived from the State Action Plan on Climate Change (SAPCC), Gujarat 2021. This information was substantiated with inputs from experts during stakeholder consultations. Based on the trend analysis and future projections, climate scenario statements were developed. 
Step 2: Risk Assessment Based on climate trends and projections, climate risks were identified and analysed according to the likelihood of occurrence and consequence. Inferences drawn from GIS based spatial analysis and analysis of relevant climate and qualitative information received during stakeholder consultations, informed the climate risk assessment. Information from the State Disaster Management Plan (Gujarat 2016-17) and District Disaster Management Plan (Bhavnagar 2022) corroborated the results. It was observed that Bhavnagar city is vulnerable to extreme heat and urban floods. Vulnerable urban systems due to extreme heat and urban flood were assessed. Step 3: Vulnerability Assessment Results from the risk assessment, along with data received from various departments of BMC, and qualitative information received during stakeholder consultations and one to one meetings, were used to assess the vulnerability of urban systems and their impact on people. The impacts on vulnerable groups such as low-income populations (focusing on hawkers, street side vendors, and slum dwellers), women, children, people with disabilities and the uneducated were also assessed. Vulnerable areas were identified following spatial analysis - Maps reflecting this analysis are included. The impacts of climate risks and air pollution on basic urban services (water, wastewater, stormwater, solid waste management, transport, urban greens) and emergency services (hospitals and fire services) were examined. Ward wise complaints, by urban sector and complaint types, from BMC's Comprehensive Complaints Redressal System (CCRS), were spatially analysed; this information supported the identification of areas that are vulnerable to fragile urban systems. For each urban system, the populations that are most vulnerable are also identified and their adaptive capacity is assessed in terms of their access to resources, access to information and their capacity to respond to stresses. Hotspot areas or highly vulnerable wards were identified through a map overlay technique, wherein geospatial information on complaints, climate risks/hazards and gaps in urban infrastructure and/or services were superimposed and analysed. 

Details and inferences of the climate vulnerability assessment are included in section 4.3 of attached Bhavnagar Climate Resilient City Action Plan. Please refer Chapter 4 from page number 63 to 104 from attached Bhavnagar Climate Resilient City Action Plan.

This report looks at the two main climate risks that Jamnagar is likely to face: Urban Floods and Storm Surge Hazard Risk.

The risks of flooding are driven by the projected increase in rainfall intensity and challenges in
watershed management. Increased tropical cyclones, along with the projected rise in sea level due to rising temperatures cause storm surges, that will damage infrastructure. Saltwater surge penetrates into groundwater, putting freshwater resources at risk and exacerbating water shortages. The specific risk profile due to these two disasters is as follows:

Urban Flood Risk: The city experiences an average of 527 mm of rain annually, almost all of it concentrated in the monsoon months (June-September). This creates a risk of flooding, especially considering the historical extremes Jamnagar has faced- droughts with minimal rainfall and devastating floods with record-breaking downpours. The situation is further complicated by drainage blockages and increased runoff from hardened surfaces within the city. Composite flood risk mapping identifies high risk (9%) and moderate risk (18%). These include Ward 10 at the meeting point of the Rangmati and Nagmati rivers, Ward 4 a low-lying area, and Ward 1 near Jamnagar Railway Station. Other wards with low risk (73%) that require immediate attention for settlements in the floodplain include Ward 11, 12, 15, 16.

Storm Surge Hazard Risk: Jamnagar's coastal location makes it highly vulnerable to cyclones. As per GSDM study (figure 18),
over 120 cyclones from the Arabian Sea have impacted the Gujarat coastal region of Saurashtra and Kachchh in the past century. The district has experienced wind speeds exceeding 55 m/sec (almost 200 km/h), with inland city areas experiencing 48-50 m/sec (173-180 km/h). Heavy storm surges cause saline water intrusion, rendering fertile land unproductive. This poses threat to city's freshwater supply and increase dependency on groundwater resources.
Investing in cyclone shelters, enforcing wind-resistant building codes as per Bureau of Indian
Standards, and strengthening freshwater supply network will be vital resilient strategies for the
city

Analysis of historical climate data, spatial information on urban geography and infrastructure, spatial dynamics of the city's demography are key to CRVA. However, poor availability of accurate data and spatial information limits the scope and depth of the assessment across sectors. Therefore, significant inputs from stakeholders were considered during the assessment. Further, sector-wise data available from the city's grievance redressal system was analysed along with stakeholder inputs to identify the vulnerable locations and urban service infrastructure in the city. \nThe key components of the Climate Risks and Vulnerability Assessment undertaken for Tirunelveli city based on the 'Towards Net-zero ClimateResilientCities' methodology are i) analysis of climate trends with respect to historical rainfall and temperature; ii) assessment of the risks due to climate hazards identified by Tirunelveli District's Disaster Management Plan, flooding, cloudbursts, and heat waves; and iii) vulnerability assessment of urban service sectors and climate impacts on population groups. The details of the Climate Risks and Vulnerability Assessment undertaken for Tirunelveli is included in Chapter 5 of the Tirunelveli Net-zero Climate Action Plan attached.

column20: Durham's Community Climate Adaptation Plan (DCCAP) sets out a vision, goals and actions to help Durham Region adapt to climate change. DCCAP was developed in collaboration with Durham Region, local municipalities, Conservation Authorities, energy utilities, and other local stakeholders. In addition to addressing its own responsibilities, the Regional government monitors the progress on behalf of the community. The process to produce DCCAP has been:1. Scientifically-based - SENES Consultants were engaged to provide projections of the climate conditions in Durham in the 2040s. This work describes the mid-term future for which we need to plan.2. Consultative - The relevant stakeholders across the Durham community were consulted on the impacts and implications of these climate projections.3. Rigorous - Risk analyses were undertaken by expert stakeholders to identify the issues of greatest concern.4. Peer-based - Best practice analysis among other municipalities identified best practices elsewhere.5. Collaborative - Experts from the Region, local municipalities, electrical utilities, conservation authorities and the community were engaged to design the responsive programs needed in Durham.6. Comprehensive - This Plan addresses six sectors in a coordinated fashion that covers most of Durham's risk areas. Proposals for addressing remaining sectors (agriculture, telecommunications, provincial roads and other forms of transportation) are offered. The 18 proposed programs in DCCAP approved by Durham Regional Council on behalf of the Durham community are: Cross-Sectoral programs: 1. Protect Our Outside Workers 2. Social Infrastructure for Emergency Resilience Building Sector programs: 3. The Durham Climate Resilience Standard for New Buildings4. Building Retrofit for Climate Resilience Electrical Sector programs: 5. Asset Protection Against Flooding 6. Vegetation Management 7. Asset Design and Service Life Management Program Flooding Sector programs: 8. Address Urban Flooding9. Redefine Flood Hazards Considering Climate Change10. Improve Flood Forecasting, Warning and Emergency Response11. Address Riverine Flooding Human Health Sector programs:12. Extreme Weather Alert and Response (EWAR) System 13. Property Standards By-laws for Maximum Temperature Allowed in Apartments 14. “Cool Durham” Heat Reduction Program Roads Sector programs: 15. Resilient Asphalt Program 16. Road Embankment Program 17. Adaptive Culverts and Bridges Natural Environment Sector program: 18. Achieving Climate Change Resilience in the Natural Environment Responsibility for implementing these programs is a complex matter, as legal responsibility and financial authority are distributed among: The Region of Durham, Local municipalities of Pickering, Ajax, Whitby, Oshawa, Scugog, Brock, Clarington, & Uxbridge, Electrical utilities, Conservation authorities, Provincial agencies, and Federal agencies. Climate Change in Durham: To account for the impact of global climate change in Durham and to predict the trends in temperature, precipitation, extreme weather and other climate factors for the Durham community, a study called Durham Region's Future Climate (2040 - 2049) was conducted in 2013. This was undertaken by SENES Consultants in December 2013 and was based on a similar projection commissioned by the City of Toronto in 2011.The study was based on the IPCC's most credible scenario of future global greenhouse gas emissions and linked three climate and weather models to provide detailed projections of average and extreme climate parameters for various sites in Durham. The projections cover the future period of 2040 to 2049 compared to the base period of 2000 to 2009 and forms the foundation for the climate adaptation plans within the Region. Whitby was selected as the proxy site for all of Durham, but data are provided for all eight local municipalities (in most cases the 1km by 1km cell over city hall). Overall, the study suggests Durham's future climate to be warmer, wetter and wilder. Data for all eight municipalities are presented in the attachment under Appendix 2: Durham Region's Future Climate 2040-2049 (SENES Report Summary). Lastly, in 2019, Durham Region updated the climate modelling to project our short, medium, and long-term forecasts. Based on the climate modelling results, Durham Region and its municipalities including Whitby are expected to see:1. Warmer air temperatures;2. More extreme heat days with temperatures above 30°C;3. Less extreme cold days below -20°C;4. Increasing precipitation, particularly during the winter and spring seasons;5. More extreme weather events, especially intense storms; and6. Longer growing season with the increased risk of pests.

column20: The Town of Whitby's Climate Emergency Response Plan (CERP) is divided into two phases : Phase 1 focuses on Climate Resilience, identifying specific risks to the Town and the community from climate change. It identifies actions the Town and community can take to reduce the impacts of climate change and the associated risks. It provides a high-level overview of the costs and economic impacts of these actions, as well as the costs of inaction. Phase 2 that is currently underway focuses on Climate Mitigation and will identify the sources of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in Whitby, as well as the flow of energy across the community. It was developed in consultation with community partners, including Durham Region and CLOCA.The CERP Phase 1: Resilience that was endorsed by the Town of Whitby Council in September of 2022 is a detailed, community-level plan for the Whitby that identifies specific ways to adapt to climate change. CERP details the programs, policies, initiatives, and infrastructure that will increase the protection of the people, places, businesses, and infrastructure in the Town. This analysis is one of the first adaptation plans in Canada to quantify the financial impacts of climate risks and the benefits of climate adaptation measures for a municipality. It is a strategic-level plan that supports planning processes and the prioritization of adaptation measures. The analysis used to support this plan represents state-of-the-art adaptation planning. A community and stakeholder engagement process complimented and enhanced the technical analysis, ground-truthing the modelling and providing additional insights on the risks and adaptation measures. The climate adaptation modelling was a multiphase approach to understand the dynamics of climate change, development, the built environment, and the natural environment in Whitby. Based on the CityInSight platform, people, places, and spaces were modelled both in time and in space. Locally, downscaled climate change modelling completed for the Region of Durham was incorporated as a key input, along with a global climate scenario called RCP8.5 that represents an increasing trajectory of GHG emissions. The summary of these models indicates a warmer, wetter, and wilder Whitby in the future. Under this scenario, the annual mean temperature in Whitby is expected to rise and will be accompanied by an increase in the number of extreme heat days. Since the climate hazards and the environment of Whitby will change over time, the impacts and risks to Whitby now and into the future will be modeled. This will be done by developing two future scenarios for the Town:1. A business-as-usual scenario, which includes growth and development without a climate adaptation lens; and,2. An adapted scenario, where measures to reduce the direct and indirect risks are applied across the community. As a result, future climate hazards will be applied to these two scenarios to gain a fuller understanding of the potential to reduce the risks to Whitby by implementing adaptive measures. The spatial and temporal analysis allows for the development of multiple scenarios for Whitby. The first, a present-day scenario, acts as the base map upon which all changes are made. This scenario represents the physical environment of Whitby, as well as the scale and probability of climate events today. This scenario is then projected into the future (2070) in two ways: the first with growth, development, and actions as they are planned today (business as planned); the second with deliberate actions taken to reduce the risk of damages and impacts from climate change. The second scenario, the adapted 2070 scenario, represents the possible future for Whitby if careful consideration is taken now to adapt for the future. In addition to spatial and temporal modelling, the costs and benefits of adapting to climate change have been captured. Financial modelling of the damages from climate change in the present day, and in the two future scenarios, allows for a comparison of the costs of action to adapt to climate change and the costs of inaction. Finally, CERP has helped to identify the necessary steps to develop a comprehensive adaptation plan that considers the current climate change trends, the potential risks and impacts, and the resources needed to address them. It has also helped to identify potential sources of funding, partnerships, and other key considerations, as well as a timeline for implementation. As per action 1.7 of the Implementation Plan of CERP Phase1: Resilience \'Monitor climate change predictions and update the Plan\' a staff person will be assigned to track the latest climate data and information relevant to Whitby and the Resilience Plan will be reviewed and updated every years.

El Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático de Cerro Navia incorpora en su diagnóstico y líneas de acción a las poblaciones vulnerables, considerando que la comuna presenta altos niveles de densidad poblacional, precariedad habitacional, multiarriendos, adultos mayores y niños expuestos a condiciones de riesgo. Estos grupos son los más sensibles frente a eventos climáticos como olas de calor, inundaciones o contaminación del aire, por lo que se busca priorizar medidas que reduzcan brechas sociales y protejan a quienes enfrentan mayores limitaciones de adaptación.

Asimismo, el plan integra los peligros identificados —olas de calor, lluvias intensas, escasez hídrica, contaminación atmosférica e incendios urbanos— dentro de un marco general de gestión, evitando abordajes aislados y asegurando coherencia con la Ley Marco de Cambio Climático y el Sistema Nacional de Prevención y Respuesta ante Desastres. Esta priorización de riesgos se definió mediante un proceso participativo y análisis técnico, lo que permite focalizar recursos en los eventos más recurrentes y críticos para la comuna.

Se incorpora la seguridad hídrica debido a la creciente escasez de agua y sus impactos sobre áreas verdes, servicios comunitarios y salud urbana. De igual forma, se consideran los sistemas urbanos como eje central, dado que Cerro Navia es un territorio completamente urbano y altamente vulnerable en infraestructura, movilidad, vivienda y servicios básicos.

Finalmente, el plan reconoce a la naturaleza como un elemento clave de resiliencia, promoviendo soluciones basadas en la naturaleza a través de la protección del arbolado urbano, la recuperación de áreas verdes y la ribera del río Mapocho, entre otros, que contribuyen a la regulación climática, absorción de aguas lluvias y mejora de la calidad de vida comunitaria.

El proceso fue desarrollado de manera participativa, integrando a la comunidad, organizaciones sociales, sector público y privado.

La visión comunal apunta a “construir un Cerro Navia sostenible”, promoviendo eficiencia energética, uso de energías limpias, educación ambiental y compromiso social, con el objetivo de mejorar la calidad de vida y la armonía con el medio ambiente.

La EEL constituye así un compromiso con la transición hacia un modelo energético local más limpio, inclusivo y resiliente, donde la reducción de la pobreza energética y la participación ciudadana son ejes centrales para avanzar hacia un futuro sostenible en Cerro Navia.

A avaliação dos riscos de vulnerabilidade em Cáceres foi realizada em conjunto com a assessoria do Instituto Nosso Clima, com foco especial nas queimadas e nas ondas de calor que afetam a região anualmente. Essa colaboração visa identificar as principais ameaças e suas consequências para a comunidade, considerando as características locais e as condições climáticas específicas.

As queimadas, frequentemente intensificadas por condições climáticas adversas, não apenas prejudicam a qualidade do ar, mas também impactam a saúde da população e a biodiversidade da região. Por outro lado, as ondas de calor, que se tornaram mais frequentes e intensas, aumentam o risco de desidratação, doenças respiratórias e outras complicações de saúde, especialmente entre os grupos mais vulneráveis, como idosos e crianças.

A análise conduzida pelo Instituto Nosso Clima buscou mapear essas vulnerabilidades, levando em conta fatores como infraestrutura, capacidade de resposta da saúde pública e o nível de conscientização da população sobre os riscos. Essa avaliação é fundamental para o desenvolvimento de estratégias de adaptação que visem mitigar os impactos dessas ameaças climáticas, promovendo a resiliência da comunidade de Cáceres frente a desafios futuros.

column20:
LBHF commissioned a Climate Risk Assessment (CRA) to understand the key physical climate risks the borough faces and to support the development of an adaptation strategy. The CRA was commissioned to align with the Climate and Ecology Strategy which contained an objective to develop a more detailed geographical understanding of the risks to the borough and the level of response required. This CRA focuses on the impacts of climate change on the borough and council, including its people, assets, services and infrastructure. The approach taken in the CRA focuses on six key sectors identified as impacted by a changing climate; (1) public health and health services, (2) public housing and residences, (3) infrastructure services, (4) community facilities and services, (5) natural assets and ecology, and (6) businesses and economy. A high-level review of the Council's transition risks and opportunities was undertaken. Risks are scored based on the period to the year 2030, when the Council aims to reach Net Zero, before controls and actions have been taken to reduce risks. A gap analysis was carried out on LBHFs key relevant strategies and plans. A red/amber/green (RAG) rating has been given for each plan to indicate the level of consideration and integration of climate change adaptation, highlighting plans where further action can be taken to enhance resilience. 

Recommendations for an Adaptation Strategy were developed following the completion of the CRA. This document was created following multiple workshops with representatives from different sectors working in council teams and some external stakeholders. The report provides a detailed report which includes current goals related to adaptation measures, with recommendations for how these can be strengthened and monitored. There are also suggestions for the creation of new targets where appropriate. 

The findings of the CRA and the Recommendations are being used as an evidence base to inform development of the H&F Adaptation Strategy. The Adaptation Strategy will include analysis of key opportunities, costs and benefits of different adaptation actions and a proposed strategy setting out the key priorities for action. It will also include a review of the council's capacity to deliver climate adaptation and set out high-level monitoring plan for adaptation.

column20: The approach to vulnerability and risk assessment (VRA) is based on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's (IPCC) latest conceptualization of climate risk and can be viewed as a risk assessment with an embedded vulnerability assessment component. It is consistent with the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) guidelines for climate vulnerability and risk assessments (ISO 14091) and adaptation planning for local governments and communities (ISO 14092) and entails five activities: define the scope of the assessment; develop climate impact statements; assess sensitivity, lack of coping capacity, and vulnerability; assess consequences, likelihood, and risk; and determine priorities for action planning. To ensure vulnerable populations were considered, community stakeholders in developing the plan included Community Development Halton (purpose: to build and strengthen the community of Halton focusing on the social impact of larger social, economic, political and cultural forces on individuals, families and the broad community), United Way of Halton & Hamilton (vision: strong, empowered communities, without barriers, in which everyone can thrive), and Halton Region (mandate includes health and community housing). One of the themes of the Climate Resilient Burlington action plan is Health and Well-Being. Nature was considered in the assessment with stakeholders from the City's Forestry Dept.; Conservation Halton (established 60 years ago to protect communities from flooding and erosion. Today they prepare our communities for the impacts of climate change, manage our natural areas and resources within our watershed, monitor and enhance the environmental health of our watershed, and create opportunities to connect with nature through recreation and education); Royal Botanical Gardens (the largest botanical garden in Canada with a mandate to bring together people, plants and nature) and local environmental organizations such as BurlingtonGreen. The assessment used RCP 8.5 to ensure no risks were missed during the Vulnerability Risk Assessment. Many of the identified hazards in Climate Resilient Burlington were also included in Burlington's 2021 HIRA (Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment) including high wind, winter weather, infectious disease, urban flood, erosion, thunderstorm, extreme cold, lightning, extreme heat, storm surge, tornado, plant disease or infestation, riverine flood, hurricane, drought or low water, water quality and wildland fire among the 53 hazards identified. The most recent HIRA (2024) included urban flood, infectious disease, winter weather, erosion, and high wind in the top 10. As per the Council approved Climate Resilient Burlington plan, a commitment has been made to renew the plan every five years, which would include an updated climate risk and vulnerability assessment.

1. Procesos para priorizar y gestionar los peligros climáticos
La priorización de los peligros climáticos en la Región Lagunas se realiza mediante una evaluación de vulnerabilidad que integra la exposición, sensibilidad y capacidad adaptativa de los municipios, con base en la metodología del Atlas Nacional de Vulnerabilidad al Cambio Climático (ANVCC). Se emplea un análisis multicriterio apoyado en SIG y en indicadores climáticos, territoriales, sociales e institucionales, lo que permite identificar los territorios más expuestos y frágiles. A partir de estos resultados, se definen decisiones de gestión que van desde la mitigación de riesgos mediante medidas estructurales y conservación ambiental, el control a través de instrumentos de protección civil y obras preventivas, la transferencia de riesgos mediante declaratorias y acceso a fondos, hasta la aceptación en casos donde la intervención resulta limitada o inviable en el corto plazo.

2. Integración con los procesos generales de gestión de riesgos
Los procesos de evaluación y gestión de peligros climáticos están integrados en la gestión general del riesgo de la jurisdicción, ya que se articulan con los instrumentos legales e institucionales existentes, como los atlas de riesgo municipales, los planes de contingencia, las unidades de protección civil y los programas estatales de cambio climático. La metodología utilizada incorpora indicadores de capacidad institucional, lo que asegura que la información sobre vulnerabilidad climática no sea paralela, sino complementaria a la planeación y toma de decisiones en materia de protección civil, planeación territorial y gestión de emergencias.

3. Información adicional sobre evaluación de vulnerabilidad y riesgos
La evaluación de vulnerabilidad y riesgos se elaboró siguiendo la metodología del ANVCC, basada en el marco conceptual del IPCC, que define la vulnerabilidad como función de la exposición, la sensibilidad y la capacidad adaptativa. Para ello se emplearon modelos de proyección climática, información censal y umbrales técnicos (como precipitaciones intensas con periodos de retorno definidos por CENAPRED), integrados en un análisis multicriterio en SIG. Los factores considerados abarcan variables climáticas (temperatura, precipitación, estacionalidad), territoriales (uso de suelo, cobertura vegetal, zonas inundables), sociales (población expuesta) e institucionales (atlas de riesgo, planes de contingencia, refugios y declaratorias). Los resultados generan mapas y rankings de vulnerabilidad municipal, que sirven como base para focalizar medidas de adaptación y gestión del riesgo.

La metodología de Índices de Fragilidad Ambiental (IFA) permite conocer a grandes rasgos las condiciones ambientales de una zona, integrando los factores de: geoaptitud, que incluye rasgos geológicos, geotécnicos, de estabilidad de taludes, hidrogeológicos, geodinámicos externos y de susceptibilidad a amenazas naturales; bioaptitud, que incorpora información de la biología de la zona como cobertura, áreas protegidas, potenciales corredores biológicos, biotopos y zonas de vida; edafoaptitud, que se refiere al uso de suelo y capacidad de uso agrícola; antropoaptitud, que contempla aspectos de uso del suelo, sitios de interés cultural, áreas de desarrollo futuro y paisaje. 


Todos estos factores se clasifican en una escala de 1 a 5, donde 1 es un valor de IFA muy alto y 5 es un valor muy bajo. El valor de IFA muy alto implica una mayor cantidad de limitantes técnicas. Las limitantes técnicas serán esos aspectos que afecten la fragilidad de un lugar, por ejemplo, los deslizamientos, amenazas naturales, áreas protegidas, aptitud para uso agrícola, patrimonio, calidad paisajística, entre otros. Para cada factor se suman los indicadores y parámetros como corresponda según la metodología que se detalla más adelante; donde el resultado se promedia de acuerdo con el número de subfactores o variables que se utilicen. En algunos factores se encontraron casos donde la metodología no era aplicable por lo que se asignó un valor nulo en algunas zonas, y posteriormente se separaron las agrupaciones finales, calculando las agrupaciones del Factor únicamente con las variables que intervenían dentro del cálculo, para cada zona que se haya definido. Esta corrección se hace pues si se definiera un valor de 0 a las zonas nulas se estaría forzando la localidad hacia una susceptibilidad alta, y de asignar un valor de 5, se estaría incurriendo en un error de concepto al suponer una susceptibilidad muy baja en lugares donde el parámetro no es aplicable. Finalmente, se unen todos estos índices para obtener la clasificación de áreas con distintos grados de fragilidad ambiental. El índice IFA calculado definirá zonas que indican qué tan ambientalmente es frágil una zona. Así, una zona con IFA muy alto será ambientalmente muy frágil, mientras que una zona con un IFA muy bajo será ambientalmente menos frágil. Siguiendo esta lógica, los sitios más frágiles serán aquellos que presenten condiciones como susceptibilidad a deslizamientos o inundaciones, áreas protegidas, y también áreas frágiles desde el punto de vista antrópico, como zonas de alto valor paisajístico y patrimonial.

The CVA is a tool that can assist in Council and community planning efforts in preparing and adapting to climate change because the CVA can reveal what systems (infrastructure, population, operations, etc.) are most vulnerable to currently occurring and, to some extent, expected climatic changes, depending upon factors such as asset exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. 

The identification of potential vulnerabilities allows the Council and communities an opportunity to prioritize infrastructure improvements and maintain existing infrastructure investments. For example, extreme precipitation may cause localized flooding that impacts a particular transit route and transit stops. The Council may work with partners to enact operational and design strategies to reduce a potential vulnerability of the transit asset. Or, identification of a potential vulnerability may help a community focus its urban tree canopy planting in areas identified as most vulnerable to the extreme heat and its subsequent impacts. 

We have assessed the impact of hazards on chosen indicators based on a series of elements: exposure, potential impact, adaptive capacity, vulnerability, and strategies. 

The process for developing this assessment included a focus group of 21 participants from the region, representing 13 cities and one county. 

The final product includes the introduction included in the page linked, three additional chapters included in the navigation menu to the left, and tools and resources developed to support community planning through the Local Planning Handbook. The assessment analyzes regional systems (transportation and transit, regional parks and trails, wastewater, and water supply impacts on localized flooding as a climate hazard). The assessment also includes an extreme heat mapping tool, as well as a localized flood map screening tool. 

The assessment includes an analysis of human vulnerability across the region in relation to localized flood risk and extreme heat potential.

column20: In 2020, the City completed the Climate Change Resiliency Strategy (CCRS). The CCRS was later updated and incorporated into City Plan in 2022. The CCRS was developed by following the BC Climate Risk Assessment Framework adapted for the context of local government adaptation planning. Impacts, risks and vulnerabilities to the City and its community were identified in a series of workshops with a staff Working Group and key stakeholders. Risks and hazards were identified based on Climate Projections, the City's existing Hazard, Risk and Vulnerability Assessment and workshops with City staff and external stakeholders. The CCRS includes the following 6 themes each of which of includes a series of priority and additional actions:1) Water Supply2) Flooding and Drainage 3) Environment, Parks and Recreation4) Well-being and Preparedness (vulnerable populations were primarily addressed in this section) 5) Land Use and Buildings6) Corporate Governance and Mainstreaming. In addition the CCRS includes a detailed implementation and monitoring plan, whose actions have been updated an included in the City's Integrated Action Plan in 2023. All climate projections were based on the Representative Concentration Pathway 8.5 (RCP8.5) climate scenario. This pathway assumes a 'business-as-usual' future in which little action is taken to reduce greenhouse gas emissions at a global scale and recommended by most institutions for climate change adaptation planning. The conservative approach allows the City to be prepared to address any eventually. The City is currently working with the Snuneymuxw First Nation, on a Climate Hazard Assessment and Mapping project. The project will update the City's Hazard Risk and Vulnerability Assessment and complete Mapping of applicable hazards in our shared region. The project is ongoing and expected to be completed in July, 2025. The results of the CCRS, existing HRVA are incorporated into the City's overall risk management framework, the same will be true of the ongoing Climate Hazard Risk and Vulnerability Mapping assessment once that project is complete.

The climate adaptation plan is based on the overall climate and vulnerability analysis and specifies which measures need to be implemented to strenghten the climate adaptation work. 

The vision for climate adaptation work in 
Järfälla is to work through knowledge and long-term thinking to avoid negative consequences due to a changing climate. The goal of the climate adaptation plan is partly to increase knowledge about how climate change affects Järfälla and to manage the expected climate effects. But also to further investigate what preparedness exists today and what measures must be taken to adapt Järfälla to the climate change. The plan can also help to accelerate the work of making decisions on strategic directions within climate adaptation for each administration.

The plan contains a large number of measures, divided by priority and hazard category. The categories identified as most important are flooding, heatwave, landslides, storms and increased fire risk. Roadmap Akselerasi Penuntasan Permasalahan Sampah Kabupaten Sumbawa

Roadmap akselerasi penanganan sampah Kabupaten Sumbawa merupakan rencana komprehensif yang disusun untuk mempercepat penyelesaian berbagai isu persampahan, baik di kawasan perkotaan maupun di desa. Roadmap ini bertujuan untuk mewujudkan pengelolaan sampah yang terpadu, berkelanjutan, serta mendukung target nasional Indonesia Bersih Sampah 2025 dan target pengurangan emisi sektor persampahan.

Berikut penjelasan tiap komponen strategis dalam roadmap tersebut:

1. Penguatan Kebijakan dan Regulasi

Fokus pada penyesuaian dan pembentukan aturan daerah agar lebih progresif dan mendukung prinsip 3R (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle).
Langkah-langkah:

Penyusunan Peraturan Bupati/Perda terkait pengurangan plastik sekali pakai.

Penetapan kewajiban pemilahan sampah di sumber (rumah, sekolah, kantor).

Penyusunan Perdes pengelolaan sampah di desa-desa.

Integrasi isu persampahan dalam RPJMD dan rencana aksi iklim daerah.

Tujuan: memberikan kepastian hukum dan mendorong seluruh pihak ikut terlibat.

2. Penguatan Kelembagaan Pengelolaan Sampah

Roadmap mengutamakan peningkatan kapasitas pemerintah daerah dan lembaga pengelola sampah.
Meliputi:

Peningkatan kapasitas DLHK dan UPT persampahan melalui pelatihan teknis.

Pembentukan lembaga layanan persampahan tingkat kecamatan dan desa.

Kolaborasi dengan BUMDes, koperasi, dan sektor swasta dalam pengelolaan sampah.

Hasil yang diharapkan: tata kelola persampahan lebih efektif, responsif, dan berbasis wilayah.

3. Pengembangan Infrastruktur Pengelolaan Sampah

Salah satu pilar utama roadmap adalah percepatan pembangunan dan peningkatan fasilitas.
Termasuk:

Optimalisasi operasional TPA Raberas dengan peningkatan fasilitas sanitary landfill.

Pembangunan TPS3R dan bank sampah di desa/kelurahan.

Penyediaan armada pengangkut sampah, kontainer, dan dropbox khusus sampah terpilah.

Pembangunan fasilitas pengolahan sampah organik (komposter, biodigester).

Penerapan teknologi waste-to-energy skala kecil bila memungkinkan.

Dampak: sampah berkurang dari sumber dan tidak langsung menuju TPA.

4. Pengurangan Sampah dari Sumber

Strategi ini menekankan perubahan perilaku masyarakat, pelaku usaha, sekolah, dan kantor pemerintahan.
Program yang dilakukan:

Gerakan “Sumbawa Bebas Plastik Sekali Pakai.”

Edukasi pemilahan sampah di sekolah dan fasilitas publik.

Pembinaan UMKM dalam penggunaan kemasan ramah lingkungan.

Kampanye warga untuk mengurangi sampah makanan.

Target: mencapai pengurangan sampah 30% sesuai amanat nasional.

5. Peningkatan Daur Ulang dan Ekonomi Sirkular

Roadmap mendorong sampah menjadi material bernilai ekonomi.
Kegiatan prioritas:

Pengembangan industri kecil daur ulang plastik, kertas, dan logam.

Penguatan jaringan bank sampah dan unit daur ulang desa.

Kerja sama dengan sektor swasta melalui skema Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR).

Mengembangkan pasar produk daur ulang dan ekoproduk UMKM.

Manfaat: membuka lapangan kerja baru dan menekan volume sampah ke TPA.

6. Pengelolaan Sampah Organik Berbasis Komunitas

Karena sebagian besar sampah harian di Sumbawa merupakan sampah organik, roadmap menekankan pengelolaan sejak awal.
Program meliputi:

Pelatihan kompos rumah tangga.

Pembuatan taman kompos di sekolah.

Program pemanfaatan sisa makanan untuk pakan ternak.

Pengembangan unit kompos komunal di TPS3R.

Hasil: volume sampah organik ke TPA turun drastis.

7. Sistem Monitoring, Digitalisasi, dan Pelaporan

Dukungan teknologi diperlukan untuk meningkatkan efisiensi.
Termasuk:

Sistem informasi persampahan berbasis digital untuk pemantauan armada dan volume sampah.

Database jumlah bank sampah dan volume sampah yang didaur ulang.

Pelaporan kinerja persampahan yang terintegrasi dengan KLHK.

Tujuan: memastikan roadmap berjalan tepat sasaran dan terukur.

8. Kolaborasi Multipihak

Roadmap menggarisbawahi pentingnya kerja sama:

Dengan NGO dalam edukasi, daur ulang, dan konservasi.

Dengan sektor swasta melalui CSR.

Dengan pemerintah pusat dan provinsi untuk pendanaan dan pembinaan.

Dengan masyarakat dan komunitas lingkungan sebagai pelaksana lapangan.

Outcome: gerakan penanganan sampah menjadi gerakan bersama, bukan hanya pemerintah.

Kesimpulan

Roadmap Akselerasi Penuntasan Permasalahan Sampah Sumbawa merupakan strategi integral yang mencakup kebijakan, kelembagaan, infrastruktur, perubahan perilaku, teknologi, dan kolaborasi multipihak. Tujuan akhirnya adalah:

mengurangi timbulan sampah,

meningkatkan daur ulang,

memperpanjang umur TPA,

mendukung ketahanan iklim daerah, dan

mewujudkan Kabupaten Sumbawa yang bersih, sehat, dan berkelanjutan.

PRK-BI juga mendorong penerapan ekonomi hijau, pemanfaatan energi terbarukan, peningkatan kualitas tutupan lahan, konservasi sumber daya air, serta penguatan sistem peringatan dini dan kapasitas kelembagaan daerah. Selain itu, dokumen ini menekankan pentingnya kolaborasi multipihak—pemerintah pusat, provinsi, NGO, akademisi, dunia usaha, dan masyarakat—untuk memastikan arah pembangunan Kabupaten Sumbawa tidak hanya mendorong pertumbuhan ekonomi, tetapi juga lebih tangguh, rendah emisi, dan berdaya saing dalam menghadapi tantangan perubahan iklim.

Dokumen ini memetakan sektor-sektor paling rentan—seperti sumber daya air, pertanian, pesisir dan kelautan, kesehatan, infrastruktur, keanekaragaman hayati, serta kebencanaan—berdasarkan hasil kajian risiko dan kerentanan iklim di wilayah Kabupaten Sumbawa. RAD-API menetapkan prioritas aksi adaptasi untuk mengurangi paparan terhadap ancaman iklim seperti kekeringan, banjir, longsor, suhu ekstrem, abrasi, serta kenaikan muka air laut, sekaligus memperkuat kapasitas adaptif masyarakat melalui penguatan perencanaan, rehabilitasi ekosistem, pembangunan infrastruktur yang tahan iklim, dan peningkatan sistem peringatan dini. Dokumen ini juga menekankan integrasi adaptasi iklim ke dalam perencanaan pembangunan daerah serta memperkuat koordinasi antar-instansi dan kolaborasi dengan NGO, akademisi, sektor swasta, dan masyarakat untuk memastikan implementasi yang inklusif dan berkeadilan. Secara keseluruhan, RAD-API menjadi peta jalan bagi Kabupaten Sumbawa untuk melindungi masyarakat, sumber daya alam, dan aset ekonomi dari risiko iklim, serta mendukung pembangunan daerah yang berkelanjutan dan tangguh terhadap perubahan iklim.

Selain itu, analisis ini memperkuat tata kelola kehutanan melalui pemantauan berbasis teknologi, peningkatan kapasitas kelembagaan, serta kolaborasi multipihak untuk mendorong konservasi hutan, pengelolaan hutan berkelanjutan, dan pencapaian target pengurangan emisi Kabupaten Sumbawa dalam kerangka pembangunan rendah karbon.

column20: Utilizamos una metodología propia, siguiendo la normativa internacional. La etapa de diagnóstico de la estrategia, incluye un análisis de la situación presente, en el cual se evalúan los peligros relacionados con el clima que se manifiestan en la jurisdicción, los distintos impactos que generan dichos peligros sobre los sectores del municipio y sus vulnerabilidades asociadas. Por su parte, los distintos peligros identificados son jerarquizados dentro de una escala de riesgo extremo a riesgo bajo, según su frecuencia e intensidad de daño generado. A su vez, se incluye un análisis de la situación futura, a partir de simulaciones climáticas elaboradas por distintos institutos de todo el mundo y puestos a disposición por el Centro de Investigaciones del Mar y de la Atmósfera (UBA-CONICET) para la Tercera Comunicación Nacional de la Argentina a la Convención Marco de las Naciones Unidas sobre Cambio Climático. En el diagnóstico, también, se evalúan aquellos sectores de la población que son más vulnerables bajo la premisa de que en esas zonas, los eventos climáticos extremos impactan con mayor fuerza, con respecto a otras zonas residenciales de la ciudad, con lo cual son estos los sitios que precisan mayores niveles de asistencia y preparación frente a estos eventos.

The City of Selkirk collaborated with the Prairie Climate Center to identify key risks associated with climate change in the municipality and created a comprehensive Climate Change Adaptation Strategy.

The municipal adaptation plan addresses vulnerabilities and risks, including changes in precipitation, temperatures, seasonality, and extreme weather events and how services will be affected.

Affected services include: government services, transportation and transit, parks and open spaces, water, sewer, drainage, and fire services. This strategy is also linked to the City's Capital Asset Management Program.

Of the 22 key risks identified in the plan, 12 tactics were agreed upon by City Council to act upon in order to help mitigate the risk in a changing climate.

El GAD Manta identificó geográficamente la ocurrencia de amenazas relacionadas con el cambio climático mediante la utilización de la herramienta QRE-Clima. Este proceso permite analizar la distribución espacial de eventos como inundaciones, sequía, erosión costera o cambios en la temperatura y precipitación, proporcionando una base sólida para la toma de decisiones y la planificación territorial. 
Por tal motivo, la identificación de las amenazas climáticas tuvo un primer ejercicio que 
consistió en la utilización de la base de datos de eventos de desastres ocurridos durante los años 2010 al 2024 de la Secretaria Nacional de Gestión de Riesgo (SNGRE). Dicho ejercicio preliminar, fue el punto de partida para los trabajos participativos de aplicación de la herramienta, esto fue llevado a cabo en conjunto con las áreas del Municipio de Manta que a través de contrastar bases de datos generadas por el mismo GAD y el conocimiento de los técnicos se procedió a realizar una identificación 
definitiva de las amenazas climáticas que ocurren en cada parroquia. 
Para el caso de Manta, se identificaron procesos relacionados con hundimiento y 
socavamiento que a pesar de que estos últimos no están categorizados dentro de la 
herramienta QRE-Clima están comprendidos dentro de la categoría “Desprendimientos 
de Tierra”. Posterior a la identificación de las amenazas climáticas, se procedió a evaluar su 
escenario actual o de línea base de cada una de las amenazas identificadas. Para el análisis de las variables climáticas locales y nacionales bajo el escenario de cambio climático SSP5-8.5, se presenta la relación entre estas variables y las amenazas identificadas. En el cantón Manta, en general, se observa un incremento en las variables climáticas. En el contexto de ciudad costera, para el caso de Manta, la variable de días con temperaturas por debajo de cero grados no es aplicable su inclusión en la evaluación.

La Municipalidad de Lo Barnechea es la primera comuna de la Región Metropolitana en tener un Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC), en cumplimiento con lo establecido en el artículo 12 de la Ley Marco de Cambio Climático (Ley 21.455). Este hito posiciona a nuestra comuna a la vanguardia en el compromiso frente a los efectos del cambio climático.

Los PACCC son documentos estratégicos que dan cuenta de cómo una comuna cumplirá su compromiso para abordar el cambio climático en el corto, mediano y largo plazo. Su objetivo es definir una serie de acciones y metas de mitigación y adaptación al cambio climático que sirvan como guía para la toma de decisiones.

Lo Barnechea cuenta con un Plan de Acción de 50 medidas concretas, diseñadas mediante un proceso participativo que incluyó a la ciudadanía y a diversas direcciones municipales. Este enfoque colaborativo asegura que las soluciones propuestas respondan a las necesidades reales de la comuna.

Entre las principales medidas del PACCC se incluyen iniciativas de conservación de los ecosistemas y la biodiversidad; gestión del recurso hídrico e iniciativas de reutilización de aguas; acciones en torno al riesgo por efectos del cambio climático; transporte público eléctrico y sistemas de movilidad sostenible; fomento de la economía circular y gestión de residuos orgánicos; iniciativas de eficiencia energética y desarrollo de campañas de educación y concientización ambiental.

Incluye la evaluación de vulnerabilidad y riesgo aplicados en la jurisdicción local, la cual considera otras fuentes complementarias a nivel nacional y regional tales como Atlas de Riesgos Climáticos (MMA, 2021) https://arclim.mma.gob.cl/ y el Informe de Riesgos Climáticos de la Región Metropolitana (MMA, 2020). https://www.paiscircular.cl/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Informe_Riesgos_Climaticos_RM.pdf

The criteria include: (i) indicators are evenly available in each spatial analysis unit. For example, the unit of analysis in a vulnerability assessment is the sub-district, then the selected indicators are available in all sub-districts in a district; (ii) the indicators are recorded in a document whose data validity is recognized by the local authorities. For example, indicators can be obtained from data released by Badan Pusat Statistik (BPS) or related agencies/SKPD; (iii) there should be indicators that are recorded periodically, so that patterns and trends can be determined between periods, including to describe future trends so that current and future vulnerabilities can be assessed. For example, researchers can ask for the opinion of key informants to map the character (type, spatial distribution, frequency, magnitude) of disasters that occur in an area, through various methods that are commonly used, including brainstorming, focus group discussions, oral history, stakeholder consultation.

Working with the region's emergency management directors, a redefined definition of risk that equals threat * social vulnerabilities * severity of consequence was implemented that included climate sensitivities, social vulnerabilities, and local Department of Health data. The risk assessment was established to set a consistent risk definition and develop a methodology, operationalizing it through other mechanisms that include state/federal reporting. The R2C has convened with partners through a series of stakeholder meetings with a technical advisory committee to standardize and define risk for this assessment. Our partners agreed upon a consistent set of threats and assets for the region, and have included drivers of vulnerability that include 32 indicators, gathering data sets to spatially illustrate the complex relationships and impacts. Furthermore, standardized and consistent hazards, climate sensitivities, social vulnerabilities and asset datasets are operationalized into each state required, municipal level vulnerability assessment throughout the region. Critical asset focus area data was incorporated into the complex modeling. The spatially organized risk assessment has already provided a significant shift in mitigation approaches and scales. This innovative assessment allowed for inclusion of hospital organizations and department of health data sets that fill in gaps in understanding shock/stressor impacts to the people that governments serve along with the inclusion of 32 unique and standardized social vulnerability indicators. As a result of the modeling, heat as a hazard ranked #2 in a county where it had previously ranked #9. Resources like cooling stations and deployment of services during heat waves were deployed during the summer of 2023 as well as subsequent years. In addition, the people-focused approach and social vulnerabilities/drivers identified are being utilized in several planning projects throughout the region. Specifically, REACH is a partnership with the City of Orlando and the University of Central Florida who are designing, building, and deploying a resilience hub with community input for both 'blue' and 'grey' skies. 
Furthermore, additional and aligned methodologies were developed for the EM departments to maintain accreditation. 
During the roll out of the assessment, the team conducted one on one workshops within each represented county to review the results, illustrate pathways to operationalize the information to drive empirical decision making as well as to engage partners and residents in understanding the economies of risk to their property tax base and their private property through a partnership with HighTide platform called ARKLY.com. This site provides direct access to the private flood insurance market. 
This year, the project team in collaboration with UCF and the R2C Risk Assessment Committee standardized and integrated the vulnerability assessment with extreme rainfall data. All analytics for the 2023 regional risk assessment were updated and automated: hazard threats, vulnerabilities, severity of consequences, and risk maps. A webtool, VMAP (Vulnerability Mapping Analysis Platform), was developed that will allow annual updates and provide future plan iterations that will more seamlessly align and link with the variety of state and federal plans required each year. Further, the highest areas of composite risk across the region were analyzed and a holistic reflection of included metrics driving risk across 18 regional priority project areas was presented. Gaining an understanding of the top five threats, vulnerable infrastructure, and social indicators in these high-risk areas allows for empirically-driven investments, activating multiple avenues for risk reduction. The R2C has begun to coordinate focused conversations across multiple jurisdictions on 3 of the regional priority project areas to begin exploring mitigation/adaptation possibilities.
Concurrently, the R2C leveraged the completed R2C economic risk assessment and again operationalized the extreme rainfall modeling outputs to raise public awareness of flood risk, increase intake of flood insurance, and increase points earned within the Community Rating System (CRS) to achieve discounts for National Flood Insurance Program policyholders.

The assessment was completed as part of the Nova Scotia North Climate Cohort project (2022-2024) and used the PIEVC High-Level Screening Guide to evaluate climate risks across New Glasgow's entire municipal asset portfolio. It incorporated local climate projections (ClimateData.ca, CLIMAtlantic, PCIC DVE), municipal staff input, and regional workshops facilitated by AIM Network and technical consultants. 



The CRVA identified:

High near-term risks related to heat events, power outages, and treefall affecting emergency access routes and vulnerable populations.

Medium-term risks related to increased windstorms, long-term shifts in plant hardiness, and reduced urban canopy resilience.

Long-term risks associated with East River flooding under higher-impact climate scenarios, prompting the need for future detailed hydraulic modelling and flood mapping.



The study produced two priority adaptation pathways:

A climate-resilient Urban Forest Management Plan (critical due to storm impacts, canopy loss, and stormwater implications).

Distributed Resilience/Comfort Centres in community centres to protect equity-deserving groups during heat, flood, and power outage events.

A Análise de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa compacta (AEGEEc), a partir de dados
secundários, teve como principal objetivo a consolidação de um diagnóstico das emissões
municipais, identificando os principais setores emissores em Itabirito a fim de guiar as ações
municipais de redução das emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (GEE) para o enfrentamento da
mudança do clima em nível local.
Nesta abordagem, realiza-se uma análise de dados obtidos a partir de fontes abertas de
informações, com o objetivo de caracterizar o perfil de emissões do município, bem como
produzir uma avaliação dos resultados obtidos para que essa possa ser uma referência na
implementação de uma agenda climática a nível local.
Para o município de Itabirito, foram obtidos os dados a partir do Sistema de Estimativas de
Emissões e Remoções de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SEEG).
O SEEG é uma iniciativa do Observatório do Clima (OC) coordenada pelas instituições: IPAM;
IMAZON; IMAFLORA; IEMA; e ICLEI - Governos Locais pela Sustentabilidade. O Sistema
compreende a produção de estimativas anuais das emissões e remoções de gases de Gases
de Efeito Estufa (GEE), documentos analíticos sobre a evolução das emissões e uma
plataforma on-line para a disponibilização, de modo gratuito e interativo, dos conteúdos
produzidos.
Em 2021, a partir da compreensão do impacto da ação local no enfrentamento à mudança do
clima, o SEEG Municípios1
foi lançado, com o objetivo de preencher a lacuna de informações
e estimativas das emissões de GEE para os governos subnacionais, disponibilizando dados
referentes aos 5.570 municípios brasileiros.

column20: Junagadh's climate risk and vulnerability assessment highlights the city's exposure to flooding and rainfall variability. Annual rainfall averages between 700-1050 mm, with extreme events such as 2,800 mm recorded in 1983, underscoring the unpredictability of precipitation. In 2022 alone, Junagadh received 1,318.9 mm over 53 rainy days, straining its drainage systems and causing frequent waterlogging. The composite flood risk map shows that 52.2% of the city's area falls under medium risk, while 42% is at high risk, and nearly 1% at very high risk. Critical social infrastructure—including 44 Anganwadi centers and 126 health facilities—are located in these vulnerable zones. Drainage blocks and inadequate stormwater management further intensify flood hazards, making robust flood preparedness, revival of natural water bodies, and improved drainage infrastructure essential for resilience.

El Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático de Quilicura no es simplemente un documento; es un instrumento de gestión territorial fundamental. Su objetivo principal es abordar de manera proactiva los desafíos derivados del cambio climático en nuestra comuna.

Este plan se estructura en dos ejes principales:

Identificación de Vulnerabilidades Climáticas: A través de un diagnóstico exhaustivo, el plan permite mapear y analizar las vulnerabilidades específicas de Quilicura. Esto implica entender cómo los fenómenos climáticos (como sequías prolongadas, olas de calor extremas o eventos de lluvia intensa) afectan a la población, la infraestructura crítica, los recursos naturales (especialmente el agua) y las actividades económicas. Esta fase es crucial porque permite priorizar las zonas, sectores o grupos de personas que son más susceptibles a los impactos adversos.

Desarrollo de Medidas de Mitigación y Adaptación: Con la información del diagnóstico, el plan establece una hoja de ruta con objetivos estratégicos y acciones concretas. Estas se dividen en:

Medidas de Mitigación: Acciones destinadas a reducir las causas del cambio climático, principalmente la emisión de gases de efecto invernadero. Esto podría incluir la promoción de energías renovables, la mejora de la eficiencia energética en edificios públicos y el fomento del transporte sostenible.

Medidas de Adaptación: Acciones que buscan reducir los efectos negativos del cambio climático en la vida cotidiana de los vecinos. Esto abarca desde la creación de infraestructura resiliente (por ejemplo, drenajes pluviales mejorados o techos verdes) hasta la implementación de programas sociales que fortalezcan a las familias para que puedan enfrentar mejor las crisis climáticas.

En esencia, este plan transforma el conocimiento sobre los riesgos climáticos en una estrategia de acción, permitiendo a la municipalidad y a la comunidad trabajar de forma coordinada para construir una Quilicura más segura y resiliente para las generaciones futuras.

Identificación de Amenazas: Analiza los posibles riesgos de la comuna (inundaciones, incendios forestales, terremotos, olas de calor, etc.).

Protocolos de Comunicación: Detalla cómo y cuándo se informará a la comunidad sobre la situación de emergencia, las medidas preventivas y las acciones a seguir.

El documento “Futuros Climáticos” (que complementa al PACCC) y entrega información adicional sobre vulnerabilidad y riesgos climáticos para Frutillar.

Lo que aporta este documento:

1. Metodología empleada
 El análisis de vulnerabilidad se hace a partir de proyecciones de escenarios climáticos regionales, considerando variables como temperatura, precipitación y eventos extremos. Esto complementa la metodología de Deuman en el PACCC, que ya trabajaba con la lógica de exposición, sensibilidad y capacidad adaptativa.

2. Factores de riesgo identificados

 * Temperatura: se proyecta un aumento sostenido que incrementa el riesgo de incendios forestales y estrés hídrico.
 * Precipitaciones: disminución de lluvias en temporada crítica para agricultura, con mayor riesgo de sequías.
 * Eventos extremos: intensificación de olas de calor y precipitaciones concentradas que podrían generar inundaciones y remociones en masa.

3. Sectores vulnerables destacados

 * Agropecuario: alta exposición a la disminución de lluvias y cambios de temperatura.
 * Ecosistemas hídricos: especialmente el Lago Llanquihue, por riesgos de eutrofización y proliferación de cianobacterias tóxicas.
 * Infraestructura urbana: vulnerabilidad ante lluvias intensas que saturan sistemas de drenaje.
 * Salud de la población: exposición a olas de calor, incremento de enfermedades respiratorias y vectoriales.

4. Integración a gestión local
 El estudio refuerza que estos riesgos deben vincularse a los instrumentos de planificación territorial y de gestión de emergencias (ej. Plan Comunal de Emergencia, Plan Regulador, Ordenanza Ambiental).

The Butuan City Climate and Disaster Risk Assessment (CDRA)

The Butuan City Climate and Disaster Risk Assessment (CDRA) is a mandatory technical and analytical document that assesses the city's susceptibility to the impacts of climate change and natural disasters.
Its primary purpose is to integrate scientific risk and vulnerability analyses directly into the city's long-term planning tools—most notably the Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP), its accompanying Zoning Ordinance, and the Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP).
In essence, the CDRA answers three critical questions for Butuan City:

1.	What hazards are we facing? (e.g., flood, landslide, storm surge, drought, sea level rise)
2.	Who and what are exposed? (e.g., population, utilities, critical facilities)
3.	Where are the risks highest? (e.g., the 20 identified High-Risk Barangays)
The CDRA is not just a data report; it serves as the core scientific and evidence-based foundation for all of the city's climate action and Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) planning.

The CDRA as the Foundational Diagnosis
•	The Butuan City CDRA serves as the core scientific and evidence-based foundation for the city's climate action, DRRM, and environmental planning frameworks.
•	It acts as a comprehensive diagnostic tool that assesses the city's overall health and vulnerability to environmental threats.
•	The identification of hazards such as floods, rain-induced landslides, storm surges, drought, and sea level rise precisely defines the specific environmental challenges threatening the city.
•	The assessment of exposed elements—including population, natural resource-based production, lifeline utilities, critical point facilities, and urban use areas—reveals the assets, services, and lives directly at risk.
•	Critically, the CDRA pinpoints risk hotspots by identifying the 20 barangays that are high-risk to all hazards, providing a non-negotiable set of priorities for resource allocation and immediate project implementation.
Direct Influence on Planning and Practices
•	The findings of the CDRA directly guide and shape the Butuan City Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP), its Zoning Ordinance, and the Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP).
•	Through the LCCAP, the CDRA findings are translated into climate adaptation and mitigation strategies, ensuring that all sectoral plans—from agriculture to infrastructure—are aligned with the city's risk profile and resilience priorities.
•	By utilizing CDRA data, the city can justify strict zoning regulations and appropriate land use allocation in high-risk areas, thereby limiting human and economic exposure to disasters.
•	The CDRA ensures that the design of major infrastructure—including roads, bridges, and utilities—adopts resilient construction standards capable of withstanding the projected intensity of floods and storm surges.
•	It serves as the strategic blueprint for developing both adaptation and mitigation measures to ensure the city's long-term sustainability and safety.
•	For instance, the CDRA mandates adaptation strategies such as building stronger sea defenses or implementing safe and voluntary community relocation from high-risk coastal and river areas.
•	It also promotes mitigation programs like integrated watershed management, reforestation, and green infrastructure to protect natural resource areas from hazards like drought and landslides.
•	Finally, by identifying the most vulnerable communities, the CDRA enables the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO) to deploy targeted and localized early warning systems for critical hazards.
Integration with the LCCAP
The integration of the CDRA into the Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP) ensures that the city's climate strategies are grounded in scientific risk assessment. This alignment allows Butuan City to:
•	Prioritize risk-informed adaptation programs and resilience-building projects at the barangay level;
•	Mainstream climate risk considerations in all sectoral and investment plans;
•	Develop a climate-resilient development pathway that harmonizes with the CLUP and the City DRRM Plan; and
•	Strengthen budget tagging and resource mobilization for climate and disaster-resilient investments.

In essence, the Butuan City CDRA translates scientific risk into actionable, strategic solutions that are fully integrated into the city's CLUP, Zoning Ordinance, and LCCAP—ensuring a safer, more resilient, and sustainable future for all Butuanons.

It includes the RCP8.5 high-emission scenario to prepare for severe climate impacts. Consultations with partners, including experts, local agencies, and international organizations, enhance the report's scientific rigor and applicability to Hue's climate challenges.

Vulnerability Assessment 

A vulnerability assessment was conducted for each identified impact statement (see attachment) to identify how vulnerable the community is to various impacts and to prioritize areas of focus. Vulnerability is a function of two criteria - the sensitivity of the community to a given climate change impact, and its adaptive capacity, or ability to cope, with given climate change impacts. 

To determine sensitivity, how the functionality of the community would be affected should the impact occur today is considered. This includes assessing how the impact would affect the community's ability to deliver and access services, maintain regular functionality, etc. In contrast, adaptive capacity refers to the ability of systems, institutions, individuals, and other assets to adjust to potential damage, take advantage of opportunities, or respond to consequences. To determine adaptive capacity, participants considered the time and resources required to restore the community or assets to its previous functionality should the impact occur today, as well as considered any plans, policies, and actions already in place to address this issue. 

The vulnerability assessment results provided a first look at prioritization of impacts before doing a more in-depth consideration of future risk. Vulnerability rankings that are 'high' indicate the impacts to which the City is sensitive or has low adaptive capacity (ability to cope/recover). 27 Medium and High scoring impacts were brought forward to the risk assessment process. 

Risk Assessment 

The risk assessment process is used to further analyze and prioritize which risks are most pertinent in a climate-adjusted future. Risk is the combination of the probability of an event occurring and its negative consequences. It can be expressed as a function of likelihood x consequence. In this case, likelihood refers to the probability of a projected impact occurring, and consequence refers to the known or estimated outcomes of a particular climate change impact. 

When determining likelihood, both recurring (flooding, extreme weather) and slow-onset events (biodiversity loss, shifting eco regions) were considered and rated on a scale of 1-5, with 1 being 'rare', and 5 being 'almost certain'. These ratings were informed both by the localized climate change projections, as well as local knowledge and expertise of current conditions. 

Consequences referred to the known or estimated consequences of a particular impact. To determine consequences, the working group assessed the 31 impacts across twelve different consequence criteria. 

Consequence criteria were divided into three categories - economic, social, and environmental. Each of the twelve criteria received a score from 1-5, ranking from 'negligible' to 'catastrophic'. As such, each impact received a risk score for each category, as well as one overall risk score. 

This is intended to demonstrate that while certain impacts may not rank high in one category, they may have significant consequences in another. As such, both category risks and overall risk scores were used to prioritize the impacts moving forward into planning. 

Based on the results of the risk assessment, the City identified 13 impacts to move forward into planning. Impacts were prioritized if they had an overall risk score of Medium or higher, or if they had an overall risk score of Medium-Low but had at least one category-specific risk score that was Medium or higher. This was done to ensure that impacts that posed a significant risk to a specific category were not left out of the process.

The impacts of climate change will affect the economy, infrastructure society and the environment. Northumberland National Park Authority volunteered to report to Government on the current and predicted impacts on climate change, detailing the risks and opportunities that are posed until 2080. The UK Climate Projections (UKCP09) provided climate information to inform the adaptation planning process.
Qualitative and quantitative information was gathered from scientists, specialists and practitioners, although it should be noted that not all individuals were in agreement about the potential consequences of climate change. Despite this uncertainty, the Authority sought to create a roadmap for adaptation actions that is as informed as possible in the light of the expertise that is presently available.
The assessment was developed around the strategic priorities Northumberland National Park Management Plan (2009 to 2014), which are: a Welcoming Park; a Distinctive Place; a Living, Working Landscape, for Now and the Future; Thriving Communities; and a Valued Asset. Each factor was assessed in terms of its likelihood by time-scale (2020, 2050 or 2080) with a consequence commentary, actions that can help to mitigate or eliminate the risks, and the indicative stakeholders responsible for taking those actions.
The Climate Change Adaptation Report identified the high priority changes, those that are predicted to take place before 2020 and where the consequences of inaction would be severe. The three key areas of risk were found to be: locally critical infrastructure; agriculture, livestock and game management; and habitats and ecosystems. The actions to manage the risks have been linked to the Management Plan Action Plan. This means that our approach to climate change adaptation is already embedded in the existing work of the Authority, as it will continue to be in years to come.
However, climate change adaptation is by no means straight-forward. There are foreseeable obstacles to overcome. There are economic barriers, because adaptation will require funding. There are ecological and physical barriers since planning a landscape approach to adaptation is a challenging task itself. There are technical barriers since Northumberland National Park is a protected area that requires sensitive management at all times, where development can only be permitted if it is appropriate. Finally, there are societal barriers to overcome. There is a rich and valuable Northumbrian cultural heritage that the Authority and its partners can continue to learn from. For example, generations of farmers and land managers can collectively bring a vast amount of practical knowledge to landscape management.
Work on climate change adaptation can only ever be a snap-shot in time, since the predictions of the impacts are estimates and societal knowledge and understanding is continually improving. This is built into our approach since the Authority and its partners will monitor and revise our work on climate change adaptation every five years. It is a fluid and flexible process that allows intervention and reaction to any unforeseen issues that emerge.

Northumberland County Council has a responsibility of care to our residents, visitors, and the environment. This duty is particularly important during emergency situations. NCC plan and prepare for emergency situations with several other key organisations (e.g. the emergency services and NHS). This is one of Northumberland County Councils legal duties under the Civil Contingencies Act 2004. The likelihood and types of possible emergencies are identified and recorded in risk registers.
The UK has a national risk register, a national climate change risk assessment, and more specific regional risk registers. Northumberland County is included in the Northumbria Local Resilience Forum (which is based on the Northumbria police area) and is covered by the Northumbria Community Risk Register (NCRR). Some of the risks included within this community risk register are expected to happen with increasing severity and frequency as the climate crisis develops further and include:
• Flooding
• Adverse weather
• Human disease
• Industrial accident and environmental pollution
• Animal disease
• Wildfires
• Cyber and malicious attacks
• Utilities failures
The national risk register (NRR) highlights that the risks contained in the NNR are not the only risks that the UK faces. The NRR looks at 'acute' risks, these are usually isolated events that need an emergency response. However,
“... the UK faces a range of serious 'chronic' risks, which are long-term challenges that gradually erode our economy, community, way of life, and/or national security.”
Chronic risks are not included in the NRR, as only focusing on acute risks ensures that the NRR remains a practical document for resilience practitioners. This means that there is currently a gap in the UK measurement and management of chronic risks (of which Climate change and ecological crises can be included). The government is currently creating a new, separate, way to recognise, assess and report these risks.
The Northumbria community risk register follows the model of the NRR, focusing on acute emergency risks. Across NCC there are many teams who deal closely with emergency planning, risks, and resilience for our communities. The main NCC teams required for an emergency response in Northumberland are listed below:
• Executive team
• Finance
• Fire and Rescue Service
• Civil contingencies team
• Property team
• Neighbourhood services
• Highways and Transport
• Commercial team (public protection)
• Community and environmental health (public protection)
• Environmental protection (public protection)
• Trading standards and animal health
• Licencing
• Building control
• Pest control
• Housing
• Planning
• Health and Safety
• HR and OD
• Adult social care
• Public health
• Education and Skills
• Children's social care
As there is no regional or Northumberland specific climate risk register, or adaptation strategy, exactly how future climate and ecological risks will affect the work of NCC, and what NCC needs to do to help communities and residents towards resilience is uncertain. Currently there is only a guide for acute risks, whereas climate change and ecological risks are both chronic and acute. During the climate change action plan 2021-2023 the climate change team undertook a scoping project, to allow for better understanding of the specific climate related risks facing Northumberland, and the main NCC teams that are already involved in current adaptation measures. The climate and ecological emergencies will cause some of the 'acute' risks set out in the NCCR to occur with more frequency, severity, or unpredictability.
